subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Related Rates: A Kite Rising in the Air

quiz.q: A person stands still, 40 m horizontally from the point directly below a rising kite. If h is the kite's height and L is the length of string played out, which relationship is correct?
Since the person doesn't move, the horizontal distance stays fixed at 40 m (so its rate of change is 0). Differentiating L^2 = 40^2 + h^2 with respect to time gives which equation?
options: 2L(dL/dt) = 2(40)(dx/dt) + 2h(dh/dt)
2L(dL/dt) = -2h(dh/dt)
L(dL/dt) = h
2L(dL/dt) = 2h(dh/dt)

quiz.q: The kite rises at dh/dt = 2 m/s. At the instant h = 30 m (so L = 50 m), how fast is string being let out?
options: 2 m/s

quiz.q: In this problem, why is the horizontal distance's rate of change equal to 0?
options: Because the person holding the string is standing still, so the horizontal distance to the point below the kite never changes
Because the wind speed happens to be zero
Because the kite's height never changes
Because the string length is constant

quiz.q: Using the same setup, how fast is string being let out at the instant h = 40 m and the horizontal distance is still 40 m (so L = 40√2 m), with dh/dt still 2 m/s?
options: 2√2 m/s (about 2.83 m/s)
√2 m/s (about 1.41 m/s)
2 m/s

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: Quantum Computing and the Qubit
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: a qubit, the basic unit of quantum information, can exist in a superposition of the states 0 and 1, and entanglement between multiple qubits allows a quantum computer’s state space to grow exponentially with the number of qubits.

quiz.q: What is the basic unit of information in a quantum computer called?
options: A qubit
A classical bit
A photon, with no further defining property
A concept unrelated to physics

quiz.q: What key property allows a qubit to exist in a combination of the states 0 and 1 simultaneously, unlike a classical bit?
options: Superposition
A concept unrelated to quantum computing
Simple mechanical vibration
Ordinary electrical resistance

quiz.q: What quantum phenomenon allows the states of two or more qubits to become correlated in ways that have no classical analogue?
options: A concept unrelated to quantum computing
Entanglement
Simple electrical conduction
Ordinary magnetic attraction

quiz.q: Why does measuring a qubit that is in a superposition of states cause it to collapse to a single definite value?
options: This concept has no connection to physics
Measurement has no effect whatsoever on a qubit’s quantum state
A qubit always remains in superposition permanently, even after being measured
The act of measurement forces the quantum system into one of its possible definite outcomes, ending the superposition

quiz.q: Why can a quantum computer with n entangled qubits, in principle, represent and process information in ways that scale much more powerfully than n classical bits?
options: This concept has no relevance to physics
Superposition and entanglement have no effect on how much information a quantum system can represent
The system’s state space grows exponentially with the number of qubits due to superposition and entanglement, enabling certain calculations to be parallelized
A system of n entangled qubits behaves in exactly the same way as n independent classical bits

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Review: Literary Theory, Form, and Voice (Days 91-99)
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand review: students revisit deconstruction, the Künstlerroman, flash fiction, the found poem, the Verfremdungseffekt, New Journalism, the palimpsest narrative, the elegy, and second-person narration.

quiz.q: What does a deconstructive reading of a text focus on examining?
options: The font and page layout of the printed edition
The binary oppositions and internal contradictions within the text
Only the exact publication date of the text
A concept unrelated to literary theory

quiz.q: What does flash fiction require in order to convey a complete story in a very limited number of words?
options: An extremely detailed, chapter-by-chapter plot outline
A completely unrelated series of disconnected facts
Radical compression and careful implication rather than full explanation
A concept unrelated to writing

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the Verfremdungseffekt in Brechtian theatre?
options: To ensure the audience never thinks critically about the events on stage
A concept unrelated to drama
To make the audience forget entirely that they are watching a performance
To prevent the audience from becoming emotionally absorbed, encouraging critical reflection instead

quiz.q: What does the term palimpsest originally refer to?
options: A brand-new, never-before-used sheet of paper
A manuscript whose original writing was scraped away and reused, though faint traces remain
A digital file that has never been edited
A concept unrelated to literature

quiz.q: What pronoun does second-person narration primarily use to refer to its protagonist?
options: A concept unrelated to literature
They, used exclusively in the plural
You
He or she

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Graphing Polynomial Functions from Factored Form
subjects.summary: Students sketch polynomial functions given in factored form by identifying x-intercepts, their multiplicities, and end behaviour, without plotting a full table of values.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Graphing Polynomial Functions from Factored Form

quiz.q: For f(x) = (x-2)²(x+1), what happens at x = 2?
options: the graph touches the x-axis and turns around
the graph crosses the x-axis
there is a vertical asymptote
the graph does not touch the x-axis

quiz.q: For f(x) = (x-2)²(x+1), what happens at x = -1?
options: there is a vertical asymptote
there is a hole
the graph touches and turns
the graph crosses the x-axis

quiz.q: At most how many x-intercepts, counting multiplicity, can a degree-4 polynomial have?
For f(x) = (x+3)³(x-1), what happens at x = -3?
options: there is no intercept there
there is a vertical asymptote
the graph crosses with a flattened shape (odd multiplicity 3)
the graph touches and turns (even multiplicity)

quiz.q: What is the y-intercept of f(x) = (x-2)(x+1)(x-3)?

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Related Rates: A Spotlight Sweeping Across a Wall
subjects.summary: A spotlight on the ground rotates and sweeps its beam across a nearby wall. You'll use a tangent relationship between the rotation angle and the spot's position on the wall to find how fast the illuminated spot moves.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Related Rates: A Spotlight Sweeping Across a Wall

quiz.q: A spotlight sits on the ground 20 m from a wall. As it rotates, the angle θ between the beam and the perpendicular to the wall changes, and x is the distance along the wall from the closest point to the illuminated spot. Which relationship is correct?
options: x = 20 tanθ
x = 20/tanθ
x = 20 cosθ
x = 20 sinθ

quiz.q: Differentiating x = 20 tanθ with respect to time t gives which equation?
options: dx/dt = 20 tanθ (dθ/dt)
dx/dt = 20 sec^2θ
dx/dt = -20 sec^2θ (dθ/dt)
dx/dt = 20 sec^2θ (dθ/dt)

quiz.q: The angle increases at dθ/dt = 0.5 rad/s. How fast is the illuminated spot moving along the wall at the instant θ = π/4 (where sec^2θ = 2)?
options: 10 m/s
10√2 m/s (about 14.1 m/s)
20 m/s
40 m/s

quiz.q: As θ approaches 90° (the beam nearly parallel to the wall), with dθ/dt staying constant, what happens to dx/dt?
options: dx/dt becomes negative, reversing direction
dx/dt increases without bound, since sec^2θ grows without bound as θ → 90°
dx/dt stays constant at 20 m/s
dx/dt approaches zero

quiz.q: Using the same setup, how fast is the illuminated spot moving at the instant θ = 0 (beam pointing directly at the wall, sec^2θ = 1), with dθ/dt = 0.5 rad/s?
options: 0 m/s, since the beam isn't moving along the wall at that instant
10 m/s
20 m/s

subjects.title: Review: Historic Experiments and Cosmic Phenomena (Days 91-99)
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand review: students revisit the Michelson-Morley experiment, the Stern-Gerlach experiment, the Franck-Hertz experiment, the Zeeman effect, cyclotron motion, the Josephson effect, pulsars, the cosmic microwave background, and quantum computing.

quiz.q: What was the Michelson-Morley experiment designed to detect?
options: Earth’s motion through a hypothetical medium called the luminiferous ether
The temperature of the surface of the sun
The exact mass of a single electron
A concept unrelated to physics

quiz.q: What gas did the original Franck-Hertz experiment use to demonstrate quantized atomic energy levels?
options: Hydrogen gas
A concept unrelated to physics
Pure oxygen gas
Mercury vapour

quiz.q: What path does a charged particle follow when moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field?
options: A circular path
A concept unrelated to physics
A perfectly straight, undeflected line
A path that instantly stops the particle in place

quiz.q: What type of stellar remnant is a pulsar?
options: A concept unrelated to physics
A slowly cooling, non-rotating white dwarf
A rapidly rotating, highly magnetized neutron star
An ordinary main-sequence star like the sun

quiz.q: What is the basic unit of information in a quantum computer called?
options: A qubit
A classical bit
A photon, with no further defining property
A concept unrelated to physics

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Writing: The Bildungsroman — Coming-of-Age Narrative Elements
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Language strand: a bildungsroman is a coming-of-age narrative that traces a young protagonist’s psychological and moral growth from youth to maturity, often through a formative experience or journey.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Writing: The Bildungsroman — Coming-of-Age Narrative Elements

quiz.q: What does a bildungsroman trace?
options: The complete history of a fictional nation
A concept unrelated to writing
A detailed scientific report
A young protagonist’s psychological and moral growth from youth to maturity

quiz.q: Does a bildungsroman typically follow a formative experience or journey?
options: A concept unrelated to bildungsroman
No, a bildungsroman never involves any kind of journey or experience
Formative experiences have no connection to this narrative form
Yes

quiz.q: Which of these best describes a bildungsroman’s central protagonist?
options: A young character who grows and changes significantly over the story
A concept unrelated to writing
A fully mature adult who never changes throughout the story
A minor character with no role in the plot

quiz.q: Why might a coming-of-age story often include a mentor figure who guides the protagonist?
options: Mentor figures never appear in coming-of-age stories
Mentors can provide wisdom or challenges that support the protagonist’s growth and self-discovery
A mentor always prevents a protagonist from growing or changing
This concept has no connection to writing

quiz.q: Why is the ending of a bildungsroman important for showing the protagonist’s development?
options: It typically reveals how the character has matured or changed compared to who they were at the beginning
The ending of a bildungsroman never reflects any character growth
This concept has no relevance to writing
A bildungsroman’s protagonist is always exactly the same at the end as at the beginning

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Rational Functions: Vertical and Horizontal Asymptotes
subjects.summary: Students determine the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of rational functions by analyzing the factored numerator and denominator and comparing their degrees.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Rational Functions: Vertical and Horizontal Asymptotes

quiz.q: For f(x) = 1/(x-3), what is the vertical asymptote?
For f(x) = (2x²+1)/(x²-4), what is the horizontal asymptote?
options: there is no horizontal asymptote

quiz.q: For f(x) = (x+1)/(x²-9), what is the horizontal asymptote?
options: there is no horizontal asymptote

quiz.q: For f(x) = (x²+1)/(x-2), what kind of asymptote does the graph have, given numerator degree exceeds denominator degree by 1?
options: an oblique (slant) asymptote
a horizontal asymptote y = 0
no asymptote at all
a horizontal asymptote y = 1

quiz.q: For f(x) = (x+5)/((x-1)(x+4)), where do the vertical asymptotes occur?
options: x = -1 and x = 4
x = -5 only
x = 1 and x = -4
x = 1 and x = 4

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Related Rates: Water Filling a Triangular Trough
subjects.summary: Water is pumped into a trough with a triangular cross-section at a constant rate. You'll use similar triangles to express the water's surface width in terms of its depth, then find how fast the depth is rising.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Related Rates: Water Filling a Triangular Trough

quiz.q: A trough is a triangular prism, 10 m long, with a triangular cross-section that has a top width of 4 m when full to a depth of 3 m (vertex pointing down). At water depth h, the surface width w satisfies which relationship (by similar triangles)?
options: w = 4h
w = 4 - h

quiz.q: The volume of water at depth h is V = (1/2)(w)(h)(L), where L = 10 m is the trough's length. Substituting w = (4/3)h gives which expression for V in terms of h alone?
Differentiating V = 20h^2/3 with respect to time t gives which equation?
options: dV/dt = (20/3)h^2(dh/dt)
dV/dt = (20/3)(dh/dt)
dV/dt = (40/3)h(dh/dt)

quiz.q: Water is pumped in at dV/dt = 2 m^3/min. How fast is the water depth rising at the instant h = 1.5 m?
options: 0.2 m/min
0.05 m/min
1 m/min
0.1 m/min

quiz.q: As the trough keeps filling (h increasing) with water pumped in at the same constant dV/dt, what happens to dh/dt, the rate the depth rises?
options: dh/dt stays constant, since dV/dt is constant
dh/dt decreases as h increases, since the triangular cross-section widens near the top and needs more volume per unit rise
dh/dt increases as h increases
dh/dt would be exactly the same as in a rectangular trough of the same width, since only dV/dt matters

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Rutherford Gold Foil Experiment and the Discovery of the Nucleus
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: Rutherford’s gold foil experiment fired alpha particles at thin gold foil and found that a small fraction scattered at large angles, revealing that an atom’s positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus rather than spread throughout the atom.

quiz.q: What did Rutherford’s gold foil experiment fire at a thin sheet of gold foil?
options: A stream of liquid water
A beam of alpha particles
A beam of visible light photons
A concept unrelated to physics

quiz.q: What was the unexpected observation that led Rutherford to propose the nuclear model of the atom?
options: A small fraction of alpha particles were deflected at large angles, some almost straight back
A concept unrelated to this experiment
Every single alpha particle passed straight through with absolutely no deflection at all
The gold foil completely absorbed all of the alpha particles

quiz.q: What did the large-angle scattering of alpha particles indicate about the structure of the atom?
options: A concept unrelated to atomic structure
Atoms contain no charged particles of any kind
The atom’s positive charge and most of its mass are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus
The atom’s positive charge is spread evenly throughout its entire volume, as in the earlier plum pudding model

quiz.q: Why did the plum pudding model, which pictured positive charge spread evenly throughout the atom, fail to predict the large-angle scattering that Rutherford observed?
options: A spread-out, weak positive charge could not exert enough concentrated force to strongly deflect a fast-moving alpha particle
The plum pudding model actually predicted large-angle scattering more accurately than the nuclear model
Alpha particles were expected to pass through completely unaffected regardless of the atom’s internal structure
This concept has no connection to physics

quiz.q: Why is the fact that only a small fraction of alpha particles were deflected at large angles consistent with a nucleus occupying a tiny fraction of the atom’s total volume?
options: Every alpha particle was expected to collide directly with a nucleus, regardless of the nucleus’s size
This concept has no relevance to physics
Most alpha particles pass through the mostly empty space of the atom, only occasionally coming close enough to the small nucleus to be strongly deflected
The size of the nucleus has no bearing on how many alpha particles are deflected

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literature: The Gothic Novel and the Aesthetics of the Uncanny
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: the Gothic novel, emerging in the late eighteenth century, uses settings like crumbling castles and unsettling atmosphere, along with Freud’s later concept of the uncanny — the strangely familiar made frightening — to explore fear, transgression, and the boundaries of reason.

quiz.q: Which setting is most closely associated with the Gothic novel tradition?
options: A concept unrelated to literature
A modern, minimalist corporate office building
A crumbling castle or decaying ancestral estate shrouded in atmosphere and mystery
A brightly lit, cheerful suburban shopping mall

quiz.q: What does Freud’s concept of the uncanny describe?
options: A purely comedic effect with no connection to fear
Something entirely unfamiliar that provokes no emotional response whatsoever
A concept unrelated to the Gothic novel
Something strangely familiar that becomes unsettling or frightening precisely because of that familiarity

quiz.q: Which of these details would most likely appear in a Gothic novel?
options: A weather report for the coming week.
An invoice listing office supplies purchased.
A detailed recipe for baking bread.
A mysterious locked room in an ancient estate that hides a dark family secret.

quiz.q: Why might a Gothic novel use a decaying, labyrinthine setting rather than a familiar, orderly one?
options: This concept has no connection to literature
Setting has no bearing on how a Gothic novel creates its effect on a reader
Gothic novels always use only cheerful, brightly lit settings with no atmosphere of unease
A disorienting, decaying space can mirror characters’ psychological unease and heighten a sense of hidden danger or transgression

quiz.q: Why is the uncanny — the strangely familiar rendered frightening — considered a particularly apt concept for analyzing Gothic fiction?
options: This concept has no relevance to literature
Gothic fiction never features anything familiar becoming a source of unease
Gothic fiction often destabilizes the ordinary and familiar, such as a family home or a loved one, turning it into a source of dread
The uncanny describes only things that are entirely unfamiliar to a reader, with nothing familiar involved

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Functions: The Remainder Theorem and Synthetic Division
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: the remainder theorem states that dividing a polynomial P(x) by (x − a) leaves a remainder equal to P(a), and synthetic division provides a fast, compact method for carrying out that division and locating roots.

quiz.q: According to the remainder theorem, what is the remainder when a polynomial P(x) is divided by (x − a)?
options: Always exactly zero, regardless of the polynomial
The polynomial’s leading coefficient, with no reference to a
A concept unrelated to functions
P(a), the value of the polynomial evaluated at x = a

quiz.q: For P(x) = x³ − 2x² + 3x − 4, what is the remainder when P(x) is divided by (x − 2)?
Using synthetic division to divide x³ − 2x² + 3x − 4 by (x − 2), what are the resulting coefficients of the quotient polynomial (ignoring the remainder)?
options: 1, 0, 3 (giving quotient x² + 3)
A concept unrelated to synthetic division

quiz.q: Why does obtaining a remainder of zero when dividing P(x) by (x − a) tell us that a is a root of P(x)?
options: A zero remainder means P(a) = 0 by the remainder theorem, which is exactly the definition of a being a root
This concept has no connection to functions
A zero remainder never has any connection to whether a is a root of the polynomial
a is only a root if the remainder is a large positive number

quiz.q: Why is synthetic division often preferred over long division when dividing a polynomial by a simple linear factor like (x − a)?
options: This concept has no relevance to functions
It uses only the coefficients in a compact, efficient array, avoiding the more cumbersome bookkeeping of long division
Synthetic division can only be used when dividing by polynomials of degree three or higher
Synthetic division always produces a different, incorrect answer compared to long division

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Related Rates: An Expanding Spherical Bubble
subjects.summary: A soap bubble expands with its radius growing at a constant rate. You'll differentiate both the volume and surface area formulas for a sphere and compare how the two rates relate to each other.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Related Rates: An Expanding Spherical Bubble

quiz.q: Which formula gives the surface area S of a spherical bubble in terms of its radius r?
options: S = 4πr
S = 2πr^2
S = 4πr^2

quiz.q: Differentiating S = 4πr^2 with respect to time t gives which equation?
options: dS/dt = 8πr
dS/dt = 4πr(dr/dt)
dS/dt = 4πr^2(dr/dt)
dS/dt = 8πr(dr/dt)

quiz.q: The bubble's radius grows at a constant dr/dt = 0.5 cm/s. How fast is the surface area increasing at the instant r = 3 cm?
options: 6π cm^2/s (about 18.8 cm^2/s)
18π cm^2/s (about 56.5 cm^2/s)
12π cm^2/s (about 37.7 cm^2/s)
24π cm^2/s (about 75.4 cm^2/s)

quiz.q: Using the same dr/dt = 0.5 cm/s, how fast is the bubble's volume increasing at the instant r = 3 cm?
options: 12π cm^2/s (this is dS/dt, not dV/dt)
6π cm^3/s (about 18.8 cm^3/s)
36π cm^3 (this is just V at r = 3, not a rate)
18π cm^3/s (about 56.5 cm^3/s)

quiz.q: At r = 3 cm, dV/dt = 18π cm^3/s and dS/dt = 12π cm^2/s. What is the ratio dV/dt : dS/dt at this instant, and what does it represent?
options: The ratio is exactly 1, since dV/dt always equals dS/dt for a sphere
The ratio is 2, meaning dS/dt is always twice dV/dt
The ratio is 3/2, which equals r/2 — volume grows faster relative to surface area as the bubble's radius increases
The ratio equals dr/dt itself, since both dV/dt and dS/dt were computed using the same dr/dt factor

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Millikan Oil Drop Experiment and the Charge of the Electron
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: Millikan’s oil drop experiment balanced the electric force on charged oil droplets against gravity to measure their charge, finding that charge always occurs in whole-number multiples of a fundamental unit, the elementary charge of a single electron.

quiz.q: What forces did Millikan balance against each other in the oil drop experiment to determine a droplet’s charge?
options: The force of sound waves and the force of light pressure
The electric force from an applied field and the force of gravity acting on the droplet
A concept unrelated to physics
The magnetic force and the force of friction alone

quiz.q: What key pattern did Millikan discover when he measured the charge on many different oil droplets?
options: The measured charges varied completely randomly with no discernible pattern whatsoever
Every droplet carried exactly the same, identical amount of charge with no multiples involved
A concept unrelated to this experiment
Every measured charge was a whole-number multiple of a single smallest unit of charge

quiz.q: What fundamental physical quantity did the smallest common unit of charge found in Millikan’s experiment correspond to?
options: A concept unrelated to the oil drop experiment
The exact mass of a single proton
The elementary charge, the magnitude of the charge on a single electron
The total charge of an entire uncharged atom

quiz.q: Why did Millikan adjust the strength of the electric field until a particular oil droplet remained suspended, motionless, between the two plates?
options: A suspended droplet indicates that it has no charge at all
The strength of the electric field has no relationship to whether a droplet remains suspended
At that balance point, the upward electric force exactly equals the downward gravitational force, allowing the droplet’s charge to be calculated from the known field and weight
This concept has no connection to physics

quiz.q: Why was the discovery that charge is quantized, always appearing as whole-number multiples of the elementary charge, significant for atomic physics?
options: It showed that electric charge can take on absolutely any continuous value with no smallest unit
Quantization of charge has no connection to how atoms are understood to be structured
This concept has no relevance to physics
It showed that electric charge is not continuously divisible but comes in discrete fundamental units, informing later models of atomic structure

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Reading: Analyzing Tragic Heroes and the Concept of Hamartia
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Language strand: a tragic hero is a protagonist of noble stature whose hamartia, or fatal flaw, leads to their downfall, a concept originating in classical drama and still shaping literature today.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Reading: Analyzing Tragic Heroes and the Concept of Hamartia

quiz.q: What is hamartia?
options: A type of happy ending
A fatal flaw or error in judgment that leads to a tragic heros downfall
A rhyme scheme in poetry
A minor background character

quiz.q: What is a defining trait of a tragic hero?
options: A character who is always victorious
Complete perfection with no flaws at all
A character who never faces any conflict
Noble stature combined with a flaw that ultimately causes their downfall

quiz.q: In what type of drama did the concept of the tragic hero originate?
options: Modern science fiction only
Silent films
Classical Greek drama
Contemporary comic strips

quiz.q: Which is an example of a possible hamartia?
options: A characters kindness with no consequence at all
Excessive pride, or hubris, that blinds a character to danger
A characters lack of any personality
A characters physical height

quiz.q: Why do tragic heroes remain a compelling subject in literature?
options: They are always minor, forgettable characters
Their flaws make them relatable while their downfall evokes pity and reflection
Tragic heroes never evoke any emotion in readers
Their stories never involve any conflict

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Statistics: The Chi-Squared Test for Goodness of Fit
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: the chi-squared goodness-of-fit test compares observed category counts to the counts expected under a hypothesized distribution, summing the squared differences divided by expected counts to decide whether the observed data plausibly came from that distribution.

quiz.q: What does a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test compare?
options: A concept unrelated to statistics
The exact height of two randomly chosen individuals
Observed category counts against the counts expected under a hypothesized distribution
The colour of a graph representing a single data point

quiz.q: What is the formula for the chi-squared test statistic, in terms of observed counts O and expected counts E?
options: The sum of O plus E, across all categories
The sum of (O − E)² divided by E, across all categories
The largest single observed count, with no reference to E
A concept unrelated to the chi-squared test

quiz.q: A die is rolled 60 times; a fair die would predict 10 occurrences of each face. If face 6 was observed 16 times, what is that category’s individual contribution to the chi-squared statistic, (O−E)²/E?
Why does a large chi-squared statistic suggest that the observed data does not fit the hypothesized distribution well?
options: This concept has no connection to statistics
The size of the chi-squared statistic has no relationship to how well the data fits the hypothesis
A large chi-squared statistic always indicates a perfect match between observed and expected counts
A large statistic means the observed counts deviate substantially from the expected counts across the categories

quiz.q: Why is the chi-squared goodness-of-fit test useful for checking whether a die, coin, or spinner behaves as expected over many trials?
options: It provides a systematic numerical way to judge whether the difference between observed and expected outcomes is likely due to chance or suggests real bias
This concept has no relevance to statistics
It has no application to testing whether a physical device like a die or coin is fair
Chance variation between observed and expected counts is never something that a statistical test can address

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Related Rates: A Boat Approaching a Dock

It stays constant at 2 m/s the whole time

options: -2√2 m/s (about -2.83 m/s)
-4 m/s
-2 m/s

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Stefan-Boltzmann Law and Thermal Radiation
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the total power radiated per unit area by a blackbody is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature, linking a hot object’s temperature directly to how intensely it radiates energy.

quiz.q: According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, the power radiated per unit area by a blackbody is proportional to which power of its absolute temperature?
options: The one-half power (the square root of T)
A concept unrelated to physics
The fourth power (T⁴)
The first power (T), with no exponent involved

quiz.q: If the absolute temperature of a blackbody doubles, by what factor does the power radiated per unit area increase, according to the Stefan-Boltzmann law?
options: 16 times
A concept unrelated to this law
2 times
4 times

quiz.q: A blackbody at absolute temperature T radiates a certain power per unit area. If its temperature is tripled, by what factor does its radiated power per unit area increase?
options: 27 times
81 times
3 times
9 times

quiz.q: Why must temperature be measured on an absolute scale, such as kelvin, when applying the Stefan-Boltzmann law, rather than degrees Celsius?
options: Degrees Celsius always give a larger radiated power than kelvin for the same physical object
The fourth-power relationship only holds true when temperature is measured from true zero (absolute zero), not from an arbitrary zero point like 0 degrees Celsius
This concept has no connection to physics
The Stefan-Boltzmann law works identically regardless of which temperature scale is used

quiz.q: Why does the Stefan-Boltzmann law imply that even a modest increase in a star’s surface temperature can dramatically increase its luminosity?
options: The fourth-power relationship only applies to objects on Earth, not to stars
Because radiated power depends on the fourth power of temperature, a small percentage increase in temperature produces a much larger percentage increase in radiated power
A star’s luminosity is completely independent of its surface temperature according to this law
This concept has no relevance to physics

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Poetry: The Dramatic Monologue — Voice and Implied Audience
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: a dramatic monologue is a poem in which a single speaker, distinct from the poet, addresses a silent implied listener, revealing their character and often their unreliability through what they say and unintentionally disclose.

quiz.q: In a dramatic monologue, who is speaking, and how do they relate to the poet?
options: A single speaker distinct from the poet, adopting a persona rather than expressing the poet’s own direct viewpoint
The poet always speaks in their own unmediated voice, with no separate persona involved
A chorus of multiple, simultaneous speakers with no single dominant voice
A concept unrelated to literature

quiz.q: What role does the silent listener typically play in a dramatic monologue?
options: A second speaker who alternates lines equally with the first speaker
A concept unrelated to the dramatic monologue
A narrator who interrupts to comment on the speaker’s words
An implied audience within the poem, addressed by the speaker but never directly heard responding

quiz.q: Why might a poet use a dramatic monologue to reveal a speaker’s unreliability or flawed self-perception?
options: What a speaker unintentionally discloses, beyond what they consciously intend to reveal, can expose gaps between their self-image and reality
This concept has no connection to literature
A dramatic monologue can never reveal anything a speaker did not consciously intend to say
Every dramatic monologue speaker is always presented as completely trustworthy and self-aware

quiz.q: Which of these best describes a dramatic monologue?
options: A table of contents listing chapter titles.
A stage direction listing the props needed for a scene.
A poem in which a duke speaks at length to a silent visitor about his late wife, unintentionally revealing his own controlling jealousy.
A weather report describing tomorrow’s forecast.

quiz.q: Why is the dramatic monologue considered a distinctive achievement of Victorian poets like Robert Browning?
options: Victorian poets never experimented with any form involving a distinct speaking persona
This concept has no relevance to literature
The dramatic monologue was invented after the Victorian period had already ended
It combined the psychological depth of characterization found in fiction with the compressed, musical form of poetry

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Functions: Partial Fraction Decomposition — An Algebraic Technique
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: partial fraction decomposition rewrites a complicated rational expression as a sum of simpler fractions with linear or irreducible quadratic denominators, a purely algebraic technique for simplifying rational functions.

quiz.q: What does partial fraction decomposition rewrite a complicated rational expression as?
options: An expression involving only trigonometric ratios
A single polynomial with no denominator at all
A concept unrelated to functions
A sum of simpler fractions with linear or irreducible quadratic denominators

quiz.q: To decompose 1/((x−1)(x+2)) using partial fractions, what form should the decomposition take?
options: A single fraction with denominator (x−1)+(x+2)
A concept unrelated to partial fraction decomposition
A/(x−1) + B/(x+2), for constants A and B to be determined
A/(x−1) multiplied by B/(x+2), rather than added

quiz.q: Solving 1/((x−1)(x+2)) = A/(x−1) + B/(x+2), what are the values of A and B?
options: A concept unrelated to this decomposition

quiz.q: Why does a rational expression with a repeated linear factor in its denominator, such as (x−1)², require an additional term in its partial fraction decomposition compared to a single (x−1) factor?
options: A repeated factor requires separate terms for each power up to the repetition, such as A/(x−1) plus B/(x−1)², to fully capture the decomposition
Repeated factors make partial fraction decomposition impossible to carry out
This concept has no connection to functions
A repeated factor never requires any additional term beyond what a single factor would need

quiz.q: Why is partial fraction decomposition a useful algebraic skill to master before applying it in later integral calculus work?
options: Breaking a complex rational function into simpler pieces makes it far easier to analyze, graph, or eventually integrate term by term
This concept has no relevance to functions
Partial fraction decomposition has no later application to any other area of mathematics
Rational functions are always simpler to work with in their original, undecomposed form

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Polynomial Functions: Zeros, Factors, and End Behaviour
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Functions strand (extension): the zeros of a polynomial function are the x-values where the function equals zero, directly corresponding to its factors, and a polynomial’s degree and leading coefficient determine its end behaviour.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Polynomial Functions: Zeros, Factors, and End Behaviour

quiz.q: The zeros of a polynomial function are the x-values where the function’s output equals ___.
options: A value unrelated to finding zeros
The function’s leading coefficient

quiz.q: If (x - 3) is a factor of a polynomial function, then the function must have a zero at ___.
options: A value unrelated to this factor

quiz.q: The end behaviour of a polynomial function is primarily determined by its ___.
options: A concept unrelated to polynomial functions
Degree and leading coefficient
Y-intercept only, with no connection to degree
Constant term only, with no connection to degree

quiz.q: Why does an even-degree polynomial function with a positive leading coefficient rise on both ends of its graph?
options: As x approaches positive or negative infinity, an even power always produces a large positive result, multiplied by the positive coefficient
The leading coefficient has no effect on a polynomial’s end behaviour
A reason unrelated to end behaviour
Even-degree polynomials always fall on both ends of the graph regardless of their leading coefficient

quiz.q: Why is identifying the zeros and factors of a polynomial function useful for sketching its graph?
options: Zeros and factors provide no useful information for graphing a polynomial function
The zeros indicate where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis, helping outline the overall shape of the curve
A polynomial’s graph can never be sketched using its zeros or factors
A reason unrelated to polynomial functions

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: X-ray Diffraction and Bragg’s Law
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: X-ray diffraction directs X-rays at the regularly spaced atomic planes of a crystal, and Bragg’s law, n times lambda equals 2d times sine theta, predicts the specific angles at which constructive interference produces strong reflected beams used to determine crystal structure.

quiz.q: What does X-ray diffraction direct a beam of X-rays at, in order to reveal the structure of a crystalline material?
options: A completely amorphous, disordered gas with no repeating structure
The regularly spaced atomic planes within the crystal
A single isolated atom floating in a vacuum with no surrounding structure
A concept unrelated to physics

quiz.q: What is the formula for Bragg’s law, relating the order of reflection n, the X-ray wavelength lambda, the spacing between atomic planes d, and the angle theta?
options: n + lambda = d + theta, added together with no other operation
n·lambda = 2d·sin(theta)
n·lambda = d²/theta
A concept unrelated to Bragg’s law

quiz.q: Using Bragg’s law with n = 1 and a plane spacing d = 0.20 nm, what wavelength lambda gives constructive interference at theta = 30 degrees (where sin 30 degrees = 0.5)?
Why must the wavelength of the X-rays used in this technique be comparable in size to the spacing between atomic planes in a crystal?
options: This concept has no connection to physics
Any wavelength, no matter how large or small compared to the crystal spacing, produces identical diffraction results
Diffraction effects are most pronounced when the wavelength is on a similar scale to the spacing of the diffracting structure
The wavelength used has no relationship whatsoever to the spacing of the atomic planes being studied

quiz.q: Why is X-ray diffraction, guided by Bragg’s law, a powerful tool for determining the atomic structure of an unknown crystalline material?
options: X-ray diffraction provides no information whatsoever about the internal structure of a crystal
Measuring the specific angles at which constructive interference occurs allows scientists to work backward and calculate the spacing and arrangement of atomic planes
Bragg’s law can only be applied to materials that have no repeating atomic structure at all
This concept has no relevance to physics

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literature: Postmodern Fiction and Metafiction
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: postmodern fiction often questions the reliability of narrative, blends genres, and uses metafiction, storytelling that draws attention to its own fictional nature, to challenge readers assumptions about truth, authorship, and the boundaries of a text.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Literature: Postmodern Fiction and Metafiction

quiz.q: What is metafiction?
options: A subgenre of poetry only
A purely factual, non-fictional report
Storytelling that draws attention to its own fictional nature
A story with no narrator or characters

quiz.q: What does postmodern fiction often question?
options: The existence of grammar rules only
The length of chapters in a novel
The reliability of narrative and traditional assumptions about truth
The use of punctuation in dialogue

quiz.q: Which technique might a metafictional novel use?
options: A complete absence of any narrator
A strictly chronological, unbroken plot with no commentary
A narrator who directly addresses the reader and comments on the act of writing
A narrator who never acknowledges the reader exists

quiz.q: Postmodern fiction often blends ___.
options: Only nonfiction reporting techniques
Multiple genres and styles within a single text
Only one genre with no variation ever
Only classical poetic forms

quiz.q: Why might an author use metafictional techniques?
options: To make the plot entirely predictable
To avoid any interaction with the reader
To challenge readers assumptions about authorship and the boundaries of a text
To remove any thematic depth

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Number Theory: The Sieve of Eratosthenes and Prime Distribution
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: the sieve of Eratosthenes systematically eliminates multiples of each successive prime from a list of integers to identify all primes up to a given bound, illustrating how the density of primes thins out as numbers grow larger.

quiz.q: What does the sieve of Eratosthenes systematically do to identify all primes up to a given bound?
options: It eliminates the multiples of each successive prime from a list of integers, leaving only primes remaining
It randomly selects numbers and guesses whether each one is prime
A concept unrelated to number theory
It multiplies every integer in the list by itself

quiz.q: Applying the sieve of Eratosthenes to find primes up to 30, once 2, 3, and 5 have been used to cross out their multiples, which of these remaining numbers is prime?
When sieving up to a bound N, why is it sufficient to cross out multiples of primes only up to the square root of N?
options: Any composite number less than or equal to N must have at least one prime factor no larger than the square root of N
A concept unrelated to the sieve of Eratosthenes
Composite numbers below N never have any prime factors smaller than N itself
The square root of N always equals exactly half of N

quiz.q: How does the sieve of Eratosthenes illustrate that the density of prime numbers decreases as numbers grow larger?
options: As more and larger primes contribute their multiples to be crossed out, an increasingly large share of each successive range of integers gets eliminated
The sieve shows that every single integer past a certain point is always prime with no exceptions
The density of primes has no relationship to how many multiples get crossed out
This concept has no connection to number theory

quiz.q: Why is the sieve of Eratosthenes considered an efficient method for generating a complete list of small primes, compared to individually testing each number for primality?
options: This concept has no relevance to number theory
Generating a complete list of primes is impossible using any systematic method
It processes an entire range of numbers at once, crossing out many composite numbers simultaneously rather than testing each candidate independently
The sieve is never more efficient than testing each individual number one at a time for primality

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Introduction to Vectors
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Geometry/Algebra strand (enrichment): a vector is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction, and vectors can be represented graphically as arrows or algebraically as ordered pairs of components.

quiz.q: A vector is best described as a quantity that has ___.
options: A concept unrelated to geometry or algebra
Magnitude only, with no direction
Both magnitude and direction
Direction only, with no magnitude

quiz.q: A vector can be represented graphically as ___.
options: A single point with no length or orientation
A circle with no defined direction
A concept unrelated to vectors
An arrow, where length indicates magnitude and orientation indicates direction

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of a vector quantity in everyday life?
options: The temperature of a room
The total mass of an object
A quantity unrelated to vectors
A car travelling 60 kilometres per hour due north

quiz.q: Why is velocity considered a vector quantity while speed is not?
options: Velocity and speed are identical concepts with no meaningful difference
Velocity includes both a magnitude (speed) and a specific direction, while speed only describes magnitude
Speed always includes a specific direction, unlike velocity
This concept has no connection to vectors

quiz.q: Why might vectors be represented algebraically using ordered pairs of components?
options: Components allow a vector’s magnitude and direction to be broken down and calculated using coordinate geometry
Vectors can only ever be represented graphically, never algebraically
This concept has no relevance to working with vectors
Ordered pairs have no connection to representing a vector’s magnitude or direction

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: Terminal Velocity and the Physics of Drag
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: an object falling through a fluid reaches terminal velocity when the upward drag force, which increases with speed, grows large enough to exactly balance the downward force of gravity, resulting in zero net acceleration.

quiz.q: What condition defines an object’s terminal velocity as it falls through a fluid such as air?
options: The upward drag force exactly balances the downward force of gravity, giving zero net acceleration
The object experiences no forces acting on it at all
The object’s speed continues increasing without any upper limit
A concept unrelated to physics

quiz.q: As a falling object’s speed increases from rest, what generally happens to the magnitude of the drag force acting on it?
options: It increases as the object’s speed increases
It stays exactly constant regardless of the object’s speed
It decreases as the object’s speed increases
A concept unrelated to terminal velocity

quiz.q: A skydiver falling with a fully deployed parachute reaches terminal velocity. What is their acceleration at that moment?
options: A concept unrelated to this scenario
9.8 m/s², the full acceleration due to gravity
0 m/s², since the net force is zero
A constantly increasing acceleration with no upper limit

quiz.q: Why does a skydiver reach a lower terminal velocity with a parachute open than with it closed?
options: The much larger surface area of the open parachute greatly increases the drag force at any given speed, so balance with gravity occurs at a lower speed
This concept has no connection to physics
Opening a parachute has no effect whatsoever on the drag force experienced by a skydiver
An open parachute always increases a skydiver’s terminal velocity compared to a closed one

quiz.q: Why does an object dropped from a great enough height eventually stop accelerating, even though gravity continues to act on it the entire time?
options: An object in free fall through a fluid always continues accelerating indefinitely with no limit
This concept has no relevance to physics
As speed increases, drag force increases until it grows large enough to fully cancel the constant force of gravity, producing zero net force
Gravity’s force on the object weakens continuously as the object falls, eventually reaching zero

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Poetry: The Villanelle — Repetition and Form in Fixed Verse
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: the villanelle is a nineteen-line fixed poetic form built from five tercets and a closing quatrain, using two refrains that recur throughout the poem and interlock in the final stanza, transforming repetition into cumulative emotional intensity.

quiz.q: How many lines does a traditional villanelle contain?
options: A concept unrelated to literature
Thirty-one
Nineteen
Fourteen

quiz.q: What structural feature defines the villanelle, recurring throughout the poem according to a fixed pattern?
options: A single unrhymed line that never repeats at all
A strict requirement that every line be exactly one word long
Two alternating refrain lines that repeat throughout the poem
A concept unrelated to the villanelle

quiz.q: In a villanelle, how do the two refrain lines typically appear in the poem’s final stanza (the quatrain)?
options: They come together as the final two lines, interlocking after having alternated throughout the earlier stanzas
They are entirely omitted from the final stanza
They appear as the very first two lines of the entire poem, and nowhere else
A concept unrelated to this poetic form

quiz.q: Why might a poet choose the villanelle’s demanding structure of repeated refrains to explore a theme like obsession or grief?
options: The recurring lines can mirror a mind circling back to the same thought, deepening emotional resonance with each repetition
The villanelle’s form has no relationship to the themes a poet might choose to explore
Repetition in a villanelle is always intended to feel emotionally flat and meaningless
This concept has no connection to literature

quiz.q: Why is writing a compelling villanelle often considered a significant technical challenge for a poet?
options: A villanelle’s length makes it the longest and most flexible of all traditional poetic forms
The villanelle form requires no particular skill because it contains no repeated elements at all
The fixed rhyme scheme and repeated refrains must feel natural and gain new resonance each time, rather than becoming mechanical or forced
This concept has no relevance to literature

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Functions: The Intermediate Value Theorem for Polynomials
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that a continuous function, such as any polynomial, must take on every value between f(a) and f(b) somewhere on the interval [a, b], a key tool for proving that a real root exists within a given interval.

quiz.q: What does the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantee about a continuous function on the interval [a, b]?
options: It must be equal to zero somewhere on every possible interval
It never takes on any value between f(a) and f(b)
A concept unrelated to functions
It takes on every value between f(a) and f(b) at least once somewhere on that interval

quiz.q: For the polynomial f(x) = x³ − x − 3, since f(1) = −3 and f(2) = 3, what does the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantee about the interval [1, 2]?
options: There is at least one real root of f(x) somewhere between x = 1 and x = 2
There is no root of f(x) anywhere on this interval
f(x) must remain negative throughout this entire interval
A concept unrelated to this polynomial

quiz.q: Why can the Intermediate Value Theorem be applied to any polynomial function on any closed interval [a, b]?
options: A concept unrelated to the Intermediate Value Theorem
Every polynomial function is continuous everywhere, satisfying the theorem’s key requirement
Polynomials are never continuous on any closed interval
The theorem only applies to functions with a degree lower than two

quiz.q: Why does the Intermediate Value Theorem alone not tell us the exact value of the root it guarantees exists, only that one exists?
options: This concept has no connection to functions
The theorem is an existence result based on continuity and a sign change, not a formula for computing the root’s precise value
The theorem never actually guarantees the existence of any root under any circumstances
The Intermediate Value Theorem always provides the exact value of every root it identifies

quiz.q: Why is the Intermediate Value Theorem a useful starting point before applying a numerical root-finding method, such as the bisection method, to a polynomial?
options: This concept has no relevance to functions
It confirms that a root genuinely exists within a chosen interval before time is spent narrowing down its approximate location
It has no relevance to justifying the use of a numerical root-finding method
Numerical root-finding methods never require any confirmation that a root exists beforehand

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Related Rates: An Airplane's Distance from an Observer
subjects.summary: An airplane flies at a constant altitude and constant horizontal speed away from an observer on the ground. You'll use the Pythagorean theorem to find how fast the plane's straight-line distance from the observer is changing.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Related Rates: An Airplane's Distance from an Observer

quiz.q: A plane flies at a constant altitude of 2 km. Let x be the horizontal distance from the observer to the point directly below the plane, and s be the plane's straight-line distance from the observer. Which relationship is correct?
options: s = x + 2

quiz.q: Since the altitude never changes, differentiating s^2 = x^2 + 4 with respect to time gives which equation?
options: 2s(ds/dt) = 2x(dx/dt)·2
2s(ds/dt) = 2x(dx/dt)
2s(ds/dt) = 2x(dx/dt) + 4
s(ds/dt) = x

quiz.q: The plane's horizontal speed is dx/dt = 800 km/h. At the instant x = 1.5 km (so s = 2.5 km), how fast is the plane's distance from the observer increasing?
options: 800 km/h
480 km/h
640 km/h
300 km/h

quiz.q: As the plane keeps flying away (x increasing) at a constant horizontal speed of 800 km/h, what happens to ds/dt over time?
options: ds/dt stays fixed at 480 km/h forever, no matter how far the plane flies
ds/dt decreases toward 0 the farther the plane flies
ds/dt eventually exceeds 800 km/h since the plane keeps flying farther away
ds/dt increases and approaches (but never quite reaches) 800 km/h, since the fixed altitude becomes negligible compared to the growing horizontal distance

quiz.q: At the instant the plane is directly overhead the observer (x = 0, so s = 2 km), with dx/dt = 800 km/h, how fast is the plane's distance from the observer changing?
options: Undefined, because you can't evaluate the formula at that instant
400 km/h
800 km/h, the same as the horizontal speed
0 km/h, since ds/dt = x(dx/dt)/s and x = 0 at that instant

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Carnot Cycle and the Limits of Heat Engine Efficiency
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Carnot cycle describes an idealized, reversible heat engine operating between a hot and cold reservoir, and its efficiency, one minus the ratio of the cold to hot absolute temperatures, sets the theoretical maximum efficiency any real heat engine can achieve.

quiz.q: Between what two temperature reservoirs does a Carnot engine operate?
options: A concept unrelated to physics
Two reservoirs held at exactly the same temperature
A single reservoir with no temperature difference involved
A hot reservoir and a cold reservoir

quiz.q: What is the formula for the maximum efficiency of a Carnot engine, in terms of the cold reservoir temperature Tc and the hot reservoir temperature Th (both in kelvin)?
options: Tc/Th, with no subtraction from 1
A concept unrelated to the Carnot cycle
1 − (Tc/Th)
Th − Tc, expressed with no ratio involved

quiz.q: A Carnot engine operates between a hot reservoir at 500 K and a cold reservoir at 300 K. What is its maximum theoretical efficiency?
Why does no real heat engine operating between two given temperatures achieve a higher efficiency than the ideal Carnot efficiency for those same two temperatures?
options: The Carnot efficiency formula has no relationship to how real heat engines actually perform
This concept has no connection to physics
Real heat engines always exceed the Carnot efficiency because they include additional useful mechanisms
The Carnot cycle is reversible and free of the irreversibilities, like friction, that reduce efficiency in real engines, making it the theoretical upper bound

quiz.q: Why does increasing the temperature difference between the hot and cold reservoirs generally increase a heat engine’s maximum possible efficiency?
options: The maximum efficiency of a heat engine is entirely independent of the temperatures of its reservoirs
This concept has no relevance to physics
A larger temperature difference makes the ratio Tc/Th smaller, so 1 minus that ratio (the efficiency) becomes larger
Increasing the temperature difference between the reservoirs always decreases the engine’s maximum possible efficiency

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Reading: Analyzing the Function of a Chorus or Narrator-Commentator
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Language strand: a chorus or narrator-commentator figure stands outside the main action of a story to provide context, commentary, or moral reflection, a technique originating in ancient drama and still used in modern narratives.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Reading: Analyzing the Function of a Chorus or Narrator-Commentator

quiz.q: What role does a chorus or narrator-commentator typically play?
options: Providing context, commentary, or moral reflection from outside the main action
Serving as the storys main antagonist
Replacing the need for any plot at all
Remaining completely silent throughout the story

quiz.q: Where did the use of a chorus as a narrative device originate?
options: Modern social media
Ancient Greek drama
Twentieth century science fiction films
Contemporary video games only

quiz.q: Why might an author include a narrator-commentator figure?
options: To confuse the audience with irrelevant information
To remove the need for any characters
To offer the audience insight or perspective the characters themselves may lack
To eliminate all perspective from the story

quiz.q: How does a chorus typically relate to the main action of a story?
options: It is always the main character driving the plot
It only appears in the very last line of a story
It comments on events from outside the main action rather than participating directly
It has no connection to the story whatsoever

quiz.q: Which is a modern example of a narrator-commentator technique?
options: A film narrator who provides background information and reflection between scenes
A blank page with no content
A silent background prop with no narrative role
A character who never speaks at all

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Rational Functions: Points of Discontinuity and Removable Holes
subjects.summary: Students distinguish removable discontinuities (holes) from vertical asymptotes in rational functions by identifying common factors in the numerator and denominator.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Rational Functions: Points of Discontinuity and Removable Holes

quiz.q: For f(x) = (x-3)(x+2)/(x-3), what type of discontinuity occurs at x = 3?
options: a horizontal asymptote
a vertical asymptote
a hole
there is no discontinuity

quiz.q: What is the y-coordinate of the hole in f(x) = (x-3)(x+2)/(x-3) at x = 3?
options: there is no numeric y-value

quiz.q: For g(x) = (x²-1)/(x-1), the simplified form and discontinuity are:
options: x²-1, unchanged
x-1, with an asymptote at x = 1
x+1, with an asymptote at x = 1
x+1, with a hole at x = 1

quiz.q: A hole occurs in a rational function's graph when:
options: the denominator's degree exceeds the numerator's degree
the numerator equals zero for all x
a factor cancels between the numerator and denominator
the function is undefined for all x

quiz.q: For h(x) = (x+4)(x-5) / [(x+4)(x+1)], what occurs at x = -4?
options: an x-intercept
a horizontal asymptote
a vertical asymptote
a hole, since the factor (x+4) cancels

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Introduction to Modular Arithmetic
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Math strand: modular arithmetic involves working with remainders after division, often described as clock arithmetic, since numbers wrap around after reaching a fixed value called the modulus.

quiz.q: What does modular arithmetic involve working with?
options: Only whole, undivided numbers
Remainders after division
A concept unrelated to math
Only negative numbers

quiz.q: Why is modular arithmetic sometimes called clock arithmetic?
options: Clocks and modular arithmetic have never been compared to each other
Modular arithmetic has no connection to clocks or wrapping numbers
This concept has no connection to math
Numbers wrap around after reaching a fixed value, similar to how a clock resets after 12

quiz.q: What is 14 mod 5, meaning the remainder when 14 is divided by 5?
What is 20 mod 6, meaning the remainder when 20 is divided by 6?
Why might modular arithmetic be useful for solving problems involving repeating cycles, like days of the week?
options: Days of the week have no connection to modular arithmetic
It naturally models patterns that repeat after a fixed number of steps
This concept has no connection to math
Modular arithmetic never applies to any repeating or cyclical pattern

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: Radiation Pressure and Solar Sails
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: light carries momentum as well as energy, so when photons strike and reflect off a surface they exert a measurable radiation pressure, a principle engineers exploit in solar sails that use sunlight’s pressure to propel spacecraft without any onboard fuel.

quiz.q: What property of light, in addition to energy, allows it to exert a measurable pressure on a surface it strikes?
options: Rest mass
A concept unrelated to physics
Electric charge
Momentum

quiz.q: How does a solar sail generate thrust to propel a spacecraft?
options: The sail generates thrust entirely through nuclear fission reactions
Sunlight strikes and reflects off the large sail, transferring momentum to push the spacecraft forward
The sail burns onboard chemical fuel to produce continuous thrust
A concept unrelated to solar sails

quiz.q: Does a perfectly reflective surface generally experience a greater radiation pressure from incoming light than a perfectly absorbing (black) surface of the same area, for the same incoming light?
options: Yes, because reflection reverses the photons’ momentum, transferring roughly twice as much momentum as absorption alone
No, an absorbing surface always experiences more radiation pressure than a reflective one
The type of surface has no effect whatsoever on the radiation pressure it experiences
A concept unrelated to radiation pressure

quiz.q: Why is a solar sail typically built with a very large surface area relative to the spacecraft’s mass?
options: A large surface area is used purely for decorative purposes with no effect on thrust
This concept has no connection to physics
Because radiation pressure from sunlight is extremely weak, a large area is needed to intercept enough photons to produce a meaningful, if gradual, thrust
Radiation pressure becomes weaker, not stronger, as the sail’s surface area increases

quiz.q: Why is a solar sail considered advantageous for certain long-duration space missions compared to a spacecraft relying on traditional chemical propulsion?
options: This concept has no relevance to physics
Solar sails accelerate a spacecraft instantly to very high speeds within seconds of deployment
Solar sails require exactly the same amount of onboard fuel as chemical propulsion systems
It can continuously accelerate using freely available sunlight without carrying or expending any onboard propellant

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literature: The Epigraph and Paratext — Framing a Text Before It Begins
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: paratext refers to the material surrounding a literary work’s main text, such as titles, prefaces, and epigraphs, and an epigraph specifically is a quotation placed at a text’s opening that frames how a reader is invited to interpret what follows.

quiz.q: What does the term paratext refer to in relation to a literary work?
options: The material surrounding the main text, such as titles, prefaces, footnotes, and epigraphs
A completely separate work with no relationship to the original text
Only the exact final sentence of the work
A concept unrelated to literature

quiz.q: What is an epigraph, specifically, within a literary work?
options: A footnote that appears at the very end of the entire text
A quotation placed at the opening of a text or chapter that frames the reader’s expectations
The very last line spoken by the protagonist
A concept unrelated to paratext

quiz.q: Why might an author choose a particular quotation from another writer to use as an epigraph for their novel?
options: The chosen quotation can hint at central themes or an interpretive lens before the reader even begins the main narrative
An epigraph’s content is required to have no relationship whatsoever to what follows
Epigraphs are always selected completely at random with no thematic connection to the following text
This concept has no connection to literature

quiz.q: Which of the following would count as an example of paratext accompanying a novel?
options: A line of dialogue spoken by a minor character partway through the plot.
A short preface by the author explaining the historical context behind the story.
A scene depicting the protagonist’s childhood, told within chapter three.
The climactic confrontation near the novel’s ending.

quiz.q: Why might scholars argue that paratextual elements, like an epigraph or preface, actively shape a reader’s interpretation rather than existing as neutral, purely decorative additions?
options: This concept has no relevance to literature
A preface or epigraph is always required to be physically removed before a text can be properly interpreted
Paratextual elements are universally agreed to have absolutely no influence on how a reader interprets a text
These framing elements can establish expectations, tone, or thematic emphasis that colour how the reader subsequently approaches the main text

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Solving Polynomial Inequalities Using Sign Analysis
subjects.summary: Students solve polynomial inequalities by finding the zeros of the related polynomial, dividing the number line into intervals, and testing the sign of the polynomial in each interval.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Solving Polynomial Inequalities Using Sign Analysis

quiz.q: To solve (x-2)(x+3) > 0, what are the critical values?
options: x = 2 and x = -3
x = 2 only
x = -3 only

quiz.q: What is the solution set of (x-2)(x+3) > 0?
options: x < -3 only
x < -3 or x > 2
x > 2 only

quiz.q: Solve x² - 4 ≤ 0.
options: x ≤ -2 or x ≥ 2

quiz.q: For the inequality x³ - x < 0, written as x(x-1)(x+1) < 0, what are the critical points?
options: x = -1 and x = 1 only
x = 1 only
x = 0 only

quiz.q: When solving a polynomial inequality by sign analysis, why do you test a value in each interval between the zeros?
options: Because polynomials never repeat signs across intervals
Because zeros of a polynomial are always positive
Because the sign of the polynomial can only change at its zeros, so each interval has one consistent sign
Because only the leading coefficient determines every interval's sign

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Related Rates: A Melting Ice Cube
subjects.summary: An ice cube melts so that its volume shrinks at a constant rate. You'll differentiate the volume formula for a cube to find how fast its edge length (and surface area) is decreasing.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Related Rates: A Melting Ice Cube

quiz.q: Which formula gives the volume V of a cube with edge length s?
options: V = s^2
V = s^3

quiz.q: Differentiating V = s^3 with respect to time t gives which equation?
options: dV/dt = 3s(ds/dt)
dV/dt = 3s^2(ds/dt)
dV/dt = s^2(ds/dt)
dV/dt = s^3

quiz.q: The ice cube's volume shrinks at dV/dt = -2 cm^3/min. How fast is the edge length shrinking at the instant s = 5 cm?
options: 2/75 cm/min (about 0.027 cm/min)
-2/25 cm/min (about -0.08 cm/min)
-2/75 cm/min (about -0.027 cm/min)
-2/15 cm/min (about -0.133 cm/min)

quiz.q: At the same instant (s = 5 cm, ds/dt = -2/75 cm/min), how fast is the cube's surface area S = 6s^2 changing?
options: -1.6 cm^2/min
-2 cm^2/min
-8/75 cm^2/min (about -0.107 cm^2/min)
1.6 cm^2/min

quiz.q: As the ice cube gets smaller (s decreasing) while dV/dt stays constant at -2 cm^3/min, what happens to how fast the edge length shrinks?
options: It stays constant, since dV/dt is constant
It shrinks more slowly as s decreases
It becomes exactly zero once the cube is small enough
It shrinks faster and faster, since ds/dt = (dV/dt)/(3s^2) grows in magnitude as s decreases

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Van Allen Belts and Charged Particle Trapping
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Van Allen belts are two doughnut-shaped regions of energetic charged particles trapped by Earth’s magnetic field, where particles spiral along field lines and bounce between magnetic mirror points near the poles.

quiz.q: What are the Van Allen belts composed of?
options: Energetic charged particles trapped by Earth’s magnetic field
Clouds of neutral, uncharged gas with no interaction with any field
Solid rock fragments left over from asteroid impacts
A concept unrelated to physics

quiz.q: What shape do the Van Allen belts form around Earth?
options: A concept unrelated to the Van Allen belts
A perfectly uniform sphere completely surrounding the entire planet
A single flat disk lying exactly in Earth’s equatorial plane
Two doughnut-shaped (toroidal) regions

quiz.q: What causes charged particles within the Van Allen belts to spiral as they move?
options: Charged particles never interact with a magnetic field in any way
The magnetic force on a moving charged particle is always perpendicular to its velocity, causing it to curve around magnetic field lines
A concept unrelated to charged particle motion
The particles are attracted toward Earth by ordinary gravitational force alone, with no magnetic influence

quiz.q: Why do trapped particles in the Van Allen belts bounce back and forth between magnetic mirror points located near Earth’s poles, rather than escaping toward the poles?
options: As a particle spirals into the stronger magnetic field near a pole, the increasing field strength reflects it back along the field line, acting like a magnetic mirror
The strength of Earth’s magnetic field is exactly the same everywhere, with no variation near the poles
This concept has no connection to physics
Particles always escape freely through the poles with no reflection back toward the equator

quiz.q: Why are the Van Allen belts an important consideration for engineers designing satellites and spacecraft that must pass through or operate within them?
options: The Van Allen belts have no effect whatsoever on any satellite or spacecraft passing through them
Spacecraft electronics are always completely immune to any form of charged particle radiation
The trapped energetic particles can damage sensitive electronics, so shielding and orbital planning must account for prolonged exposure to this radiation
This concept has no relevance to physics

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Performance: Slam Poetry and the Oral Poetic Tradition
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: slam poetry is a competitive, performance-based poetic form that emphasizes rhythm, voice, and direct audience engagement, drawing on a long oral poetic tradition in which sound and delivery are as central to meaning as the words on a page.

quiz.q: What distinguishes slam poetry as a form of poetic performance?
options: It is competitive and performance-based, emphasizing rhythm, voice, and direct engagement with a live audience
It follows an unchanging, fixed rhyme scheme identical to the sonnet
A concept unrelated to literature
It is intended to be read silently and never performed aloud under any circumstances

quiz.q: In the oral poetic tradition that informs slam poetry, what is emphasized alongside the literal words of a poem?
options: A concept unrelated to the oral poetic tradition
Only the poem’s exact appearance on a printed page
The specific font used when the poem is eventually published
Sound, rhythm, and delivery, which are treated as central to the poem’s meaning

quiz.q: Which of these best describes a defining feature of a slam poetry competition?
options: Poets compete by translating a classic poem into a foreign language.
Poets perform original work live before an audience and are scored by judges or audience response.
Poets are ranked based solely on the length of their poems.
Poets submit anonymous manuscripts that are judged without ever being read aloud.

quiz.q: Why might a slam poet make deliberate choices about vocal pacing, volume, and emphasis that would not be captured by simply reading the poem’s text on a page?
options: This concept has no connection to literature
A poem’s meaning is always completely unaffected by any choices made in its live performance
Performance elements like pacing and emphasis actively shape how the audience experiences meaning and emotion in the moment of delivery
Vocal delivery is considered entirely irrelevant to how a slam poem communicates its meaning

quiz.q: Why is slam poetry sometimes described as reviving or extending a much older oral poetic tradition, despite being a relatively recent competitive form?
options: Oral poetic traditions never placed any importance on how a poem was performed aloud
Slam poetry has no meaningful connection to any earlier oral tradition of poetry
This concept has no relevance to literature
Like ancient oral poetry, it prioritizes live voice, memory, and immediate audience connection over a poem’s existence as a fixed printed text

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Number Theory: Perfect Numbers and Mersenne Primes
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: a perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors, and every known even perfect number is generated from a Mersenne prime of the form 2^p − 1 through the Euclid-Euler formula 2^(p−1) times (2^p − 1).

quiz.q: What defines a perfect number in terms of its proper divisors (the divisors excluding the number itself)?
options: It has no proper divisors of any kind other than 1
It is always an odd number with exactly three divisors
The sum of its proper divisors equals the number itself
A concept unrelated to number theory

quiz.q: What are the proper divisors of 6, and what do they sum to, confirming that 6 is a perfect number?
options: 1, 2, 3, and 6, which sum to 12
A concept unrelated to perfect numbers
Only 1 and 6, which sum to 7
1, 2, and 3, which sum to 6

quiz.q: A Mersenne prime takes the form 2^p − 1 for prime p. What is 2^5 − 1, and is it prime?
options: 32, and it is not prime
31, and it is not prime
A concept unrelated to Mersenne primes
31, and it is prime

quiz.q: Using the Euclid-Euler formula 2^(p−1) × (2^p − 1) with the Mersenne prime found from p = 5 (where 2^5 − 1 = 31), what even perfect number is generated?
Why does the Euclid-Euler theorem establish such a tight link between even perfect numbers and Mersenne primes?
options: The Euclid-Euler theorem shows that even perfect numbers have no relationship whatsoever to Mersenne primes
This concept has no relevance to number theory
Perfect numbers and Mersenne primes were proven to be completely unrelated concepts
It proves that every even perfect number must arise from a Mersenne prime in this exact form, and conversely that every Mersenne prime generates an even perfect number this way

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Related Rates: A Growing Sand Pile
subjects.summary: Sand poured from a conveyor belt builds a conical pile whose height and base radius stay in a fixed ratio. You'll express the volume in terms of height alone, then find how fast the pile is growing taller.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Related Rates: A Growing Sand Pile

quiz.q: As sand piles up, its shape stays a cone where the base radius r is always exactly twice the height h. Which equation expresses this?
options: r = h + 2
r = 2h
r = h/2

quiz.q: Substituting r = 2h into V = (1/3)πr^2h gives the volume purely in terms of h. Which is correct?
options: V = (4/3)πh^3 (the sphere volume formula)

quiz.q: Differentiating V = (4π/3)h^3 with respect to time t gives which equation?
options: dV/dt = (4π/3)h^3
dV/dt = 12πh^2(dh/dt)
dV/dt = 4πh^2(dh/dt)
dV/dt = 4πh(dh/dt)

quiz.q: Sand is poured onto the pile at dV/dt = 6 m^3/min. How fast is the pile's height increasing at the instant h = 2 m?
options: 3/(8π) m/min (about 0.119 m/min)
1/(8π) m/min (about 0.040 m/min)
3/(4π) m/min (about 0.239 m/min)
-3/(8π) m/min (about -0.119 m/min)

quiz.q: As the sand pile grows taller (h increasing) while dV/dt stays constant at 6 m^3/min, what happens to dh/dt?
options: dh/dt stays constant, since dV/dt is constant
dh/dt decreases as h increases, since dh/dt = dV/dt/(4πh^2) is inversely proportional to h^2
dh/dt increases as h increases
dh/dt depends only on the fixed ratio r = 2h, not on the current height h

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: Electrostatic Shielding and the Faraday Cage
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: a Faraday cage is a conducting enclosure in which free charges redistribute themselves so that the electric field inside remains zero, shielding the interior from external static electric fields and time-varying electromagnetic interference.

quiz.q: What happens to the electric field inside a conducting enclosure, such as a Faraday cage, once free charges have redistributed themselves in the presence of an external field?
options: The electric field inside the enclosure becomes zero
The electric field inside becomes far stronger than the field outside
The electric field inside remains completely unaffected by the external field
A concept unrelated to physics

quiz.q: What allows the free charges within a conductor forming a Faraday cage to cancel an external electric field on the inside?
options: The free charges redistribute themselves on the conductor’s surface until their own field exactly cancels the external field within the enclosure
A concept unrelated to the Faraday cage
The conductor absorbs and permanently destroys the external electric field
The conductor’s atoms physically rearrange themselves into an entirely different material

quiz.q: Which of these is a practical everyday example that relies on the Faraday cage principle for shielding?
options: A wooden table that blocks all external electric fields completely.
A metal elevator or car body that can weaken cell phone signals and shield occupants from external electric fields.
