A rubber balloon that perfectly shields electric fields from passing through.
An insulated glass window that allows electric fields to pass through freely.

quiz.q: Why does a Faraday cage need to be made of a conducting material, such as metal, rather than an insulator, to effectively shield its interior?
options: This concept has no connection to physics
Insulating materials are always more effective at shielding electric fields than conductors
The material used has no effect whatsoever on whether shielding occurs
Only a conductor allows free charges to move and redistribute quickly enough to cancel the external field within the enclosure

quiz.q: Why can a Faraday cage still provide meaningful shielding even if it is built as a mesh or grid rather than a completely solid, sealed enclosure?
options: This concept has no relevance to physics
Shielding effectiveness has no relationship to the size of any gaps in the enclosure
As long as the gaps in the mesh are small compared to the wavelength of the interfering field, the mesh behaves similarly to a solid conducting surface for shielding purposes
A mesh or grid enclosure never provides any shielding at all, regardless of the size of its gaps

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Reading: Analyzing Stream of Consciousness Narration
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Language strand: stream of consciousness is a narrative technique that presents a characters continuous flow of thoughts, feelings, and impressions in real time, often with looser sentence structure, to immerse the reader directly in the characters mind.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Reading: Analyzing Stream of Consciousness Narration

quiz.q: What does stream of consciousness narration attempt to capture?
options: A strict, chronological summary of an entire plot
Only a characters physical actions with no inner thought at all
A list of unrelated facts with no connection to any character
A characters continuous flow of thoughts and impressions as they occur

quiz.q: What stylistic feature often characterizes stream of consciousness writing?
options: Strict, formally outlined paragraphs with no variation
Looser, less structured sentences that mimic the movement of thought
Only dialogue, with no narration of any kind
Numbered lists replacing all prose

quiz.q: Why might an author choose stream of consciousness over a more traditional narrative style?
options: To remove any sense of character from the narrative
To make the story as impersonal and distant as possible
To immerse readers directly in a characters inner experience
To avoid ever describing a characters thoughts

quiz.q: Stream of consciousness narration is most closely associated with representing which aspect of a character?
options: Their internal, psychological experience
Their financial situation only
Their physical appearance only
Their family history exclusively

quiz.q: Why can stream of consciousness passages sometimes feel challenging to read?
options: These passages are always written with extremely simple vocabulary
They never include any emotional content whatsoever
They are always the shortest passages in a text
The thoughts may jump between ideas without the usual transitions of conventional narration

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Discrete Math: The Inclusion-Exclusion Principle
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: the inclusion-exclusion principle counts the size of a union of overlapping sets by adding the sizes of the individual sets, then subtracting the sizes of their pairwise intersections, and adding back higher-order intersections to correct for overcounting.

quiz.q: What problem does the inclusion-exclusion principle solve when counting the elements in a union of overlapping sets?
options: It counts only the elements that belong to none of the sets involved
It corrects for elements counted more than once because they belong to more than one set
It ignores every set except for the single largest one
A concept unrelated to discrete math

quiz.q: For two overlapping sets A and B, what is the formula given by inclusion-exclusion for the size of their union?
options: |A| × |B|, with no subtraction involved
A concept unrelated to inclusion-exclusion

quiz.q: In a class of 30 students, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish, and 8 study both. Using inclusion-exclusion, how many students study at least one of the two languages?
Why does simply adding |A| + |B| overcount the number of elements in the union of two overlapping sets A and B?
options: Elements belonging to both sets get counted once within |A| and again within |B|, so they are counted twice instead of once
This concept has no connection to discrete math
Overlapping sets never contain any elements that would be counted more than once
Adding |A| + |B| always undercounts the true size of the union, never overcounts it

quiz.q: Why does extending inclusion-exclusion to three overlapping sets require adding back the size of the triple intersection |A ∩ B ∩ C| after subtracting all three pairwise intersections?
options: The triple intersection term is always irrelevant and never needs to be included in any inclusion-exclusion calculation
Extending inclusion-exclusion to three sets requires subtracting the triple intersection twice more, not adding it back
Elements belonging to all three sets get subtracted three times during the pairwise-intersection step, so they must be added back once to be counted correctly overall
This concept has no relevance to discrete math

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Trigonometric Identities: Double-Angle Formulas
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: double-angle formulas express trigonometric functions of twice an angle, such as sin(2x) equals 2 sin(x) cos(x), in terms of functions of the original angle.

quiz.q: What does the double-angle formula for sine express?
options: A concept unrelated to trigonometry
The area of a triangle
Only the value of x itself
sin(2x) in terms of sin(x) and cos(x)

quiz.q: What is the double-angle identity for sine?
options: sin(2x) = 2 sin(x) cos(x)
sin(2x) = 2 sin(x)
sin(2x) = cos(x) squared
sin(2x) = sin(x) + cos(x)

quiz.q: Can double-angle formulas help simplify a trigonometric expression involving 2x?
options: Double-angle formulas only apply to angles smaller than 2x
No, double-angle formulas never simplify any expression
A concept unrelated to trigonometric identities
Yes

quiz.q: Why might a double-angle formula be useful when solving a trigonometric equation that contains both sin(x) and sin(2x)?
options: Double-angle formulas never help when solving equations with multiple angle measures
Equations with sin(2x) can never be simplified using any identity
This concept has no connection to math
Rewriting sin(2x) in terms of sin(x) and cos(x) allows the whole equation to be expressed using a single angle

quiz.q: Why are trigonometric identities like the double-angle formulas useful tools in calculus and physics applications?
options: Trigonometric identities have no application outside of pure geometry problems
Calculus and physics never involve any trigonometric expressions
This concept has no relevance to trigonometry
They allow complex trigonometric expressions to be rewritten in simpler, more manageable forms

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: Eddy Currents and Lenz’s Law in Action
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: eddy currents are swirling loops of induced current that form within a conductor when it experiences a changing magnetic flux, and Lenz’s law dictates that these induced currents always flow in a direction that opposes the change producing them, creating a braking effect.

quiz.q: What are eddy currents, as they form within a solid conductor experiencing a changing magnetic flux?
options: Swirling loops of induced electric current within the conductor
A type of mechanical wave travelling through the conductor’s surface
A steady, unchanging flow of current in a single straight line
A concept unrelated to physics

quiz.q: According to Lenz’s law, in what direction do induced eddy currents flow relative to the change in magnetic flux that produces them?
options: In a direction that always reinforces and strengthens the change producing them
A concept unrelated to Lenz’s law
In a completely random direction unrelated to the change producing them
In a direction that opposes the change producing them

quiz.q: Why does a strong magnet dropped down a thick copper pipe fall noticeably slower than it would in free fall, even though copper is not magnetic?
options: The magnet’s changing flux induces eddy currents in the copper, and by Lenz’s law those currents create a magnetic force opposing the magnet’s motion
A concept unrelated to this scenario
Copper is actually magnetic and directly attracts the falling magnet, slowing it down
The magnet’s speed has no relationship to any electric current induced within the pipe

quiz.q: Why do many high-speed trains and roller coasters use eddy current brakes instead of relying solely on traditional friction brakes?
options: This concept has no connection to physics
Eddy current brakes function by directly attracting the vehicle backward using a permanent, unchanging magnetic force
Eddy current braking is contactless, reducing mechanical wear while still converting kinetic energy into heat through induced currents opposing motion
Eddy current braking requires direct physical contact and causes more wear than a friction brake

quiz.q: Why are transformer cores often laminated (built from thin, insulated sheets) rather than made from a single solid block of metal?
options: Lamination breaks up the paths available for eddy currents to circulate, reducing the energy wasted as heat within the core
Lamination is used purely to reduce the transformer’s overall weight, with no effect on eddy currents
A solid metal core always produces fewer eddy currents than a laminated one
This concept has no relevance to physics

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Writing: Writing a Research Proposal
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Language strand: a research proposal outlines a planned investigation before the work begins, stating a clear research question, explaining its significance, and describing the methods a writer intends to use to find an answer.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Writing: Writing a Research Proposal

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a research proposal?
options: To summarize research that was completed many years earlier
To criticize research conducted by other people
To replace the need for any research question
To outline a planned investigation before the research work begins

quiz.q: What should a strong research proposal clearly state?
options: An unrelated list of personal hobbies
The final answer before any research occurs
A summary of an entirely unrelated topic
A specific, focused research question

quiz.q: Why do research proposals typically explain the significance of a topic?
options: Significance is never a relevant consideration in research
To show readers why the investigation is worth pursuing
To avoid stating any purpose for the research
To make the proposal as confusing as possible

quiz.q: What part of a research proposal describes how the investigation will be carried out?
options: The title page alone
The methods section
The index at the very end
The dedication page

quiz.q: Why might a student write a research proposal before starting a larger project?
options: To plan the scope and direction of the project and get feedback early
To guarantee an identical result to every other students project
Proposals are only ever written after a project is finished
Research proposals serve no planning purpose whatsoever

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Factoring Sums and Differences of Cubes
subjects.summary: Students learn and apply the sum-of-cubes and difference-of-cubes factoring patterns to fully factor cubic binomials.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Factoring Sums and Differences of Cubes

quiz.q: The factoring pattern for a³ + b³ is:
options: (a+b)(a²+ab+b²)
(a+b)³
(a+b)(a²-ab+b²)
(a-b)(a²+ab+b²)

quiz.q: The factoring pattern for a³ - b³ is:
options: (a-b)(a²+ab+b²)
(a-b)³
(a+b)(a²-ab+b²)
(a-b)(a²-ab+b²)

quiz.q: Factor x³ + 27 completely.
Factor 8x³ - 1 completely.
The mnemonic 'SOAP' for the sign pattern in cube factoring stands for:
options: Subtract, Overlap, Add, Prove
Square, Order, Add, Product
Sum, Only, Add, Product
Same, Opposite, Always Positive

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Functions: Composition of Functions
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: function composition combines two functions by applying one function to the output of another, written as f(g(x)), evaluating g(x) first.

quiz.q: In the composition f(g(x)), which function is evaluated first?
options: A concept unrelated to function composition
f(x)
g(x)
Neither function is ever evaluated

quiz.q: If f(x) = x + 3 and g(x) = 2x, what is f(g(2))?
Does function composition combine two functions by using the output of one as the input of the other?
options: Yes
Composition always adds the two functions together instead
A concept unrelated to function composition
No, function composition never uses one function’s output as another’s input

quiz.q: Why is the order of functions important when evaluating a composition like f(g(x))?
options: f(g(x)) and g(f(x)) always produce exactly the same result
This concept has no connection to math
The order of functions never affects the result of a composition
Changing the order can produce a completely different result, since g(x) is evaluated before applying f

quiz.q: Why might function composition be useful for modelling a real-world process with multiple sequential steps, such as a discount followed by a tax?
options: Function composition has no application to modelling multi-step real-world processes
This concept has no connection to functions
Each function can represent one step, and composing them models applying the steps in the correct sequential order
Multi-step processes can never be represented using function composition

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Davisson-Germer Experiment and Electron Diffraction
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Davisson-Germer experiment demonstrated that electrons produce diffraction patterns when scattered off a crystal, providing direct experimental evidence for the wave nature of matter predicted by de Broglies hypothesis.

quiz.q: What did the Davisson-Germer experiment demonstrate?
options: That light behaves only as a particle with no wave nature
That electrons have no measurable properties at all
That protons are the only particles with wave properties
That electrons produce diffraction patterns, showing wave-like behaviour

quiz.q: What material did the experiment use to scatter electrons?
options: A sample of liquid mercury
A vacuum with no material at all
A block of pure water
A nickel crystal

quiz.q: Which earlier hypothesis did this experiment provide evidence for?
options: Newtons laws of motion
The law of conservation of energy
The de Broglie hypothesis of matter waves
Keplers laws of planetary motion

quiz.q: Why was the Davisson-Germer experiment significant for quantum physics?
options: It had no connection to quantum theory
It showed that electrons behave purely as classical particles with no wave nature
It provided direct experimental confirmation that particles can behave like waves
It disproved the existence of electrons entirely

quiz.q: The diffraction pattern observed in this experiment is similar to what other well-known phenomenon?
options: The refraction of sound through air
The reflection of light off a flat mirror
The absorption of heat by a metal rod
The diffraction of light waves through a crystal lattice

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literary Theory: New Criticism and Close Reading
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: New Criticism emphasizes close reading of a text on its own terms, focusing on elements like structure, imagery, and language while deliberately setting aside the authors biography and historical context.

quiz.q: What does New Criticism emphasize when analyzing a text?
options: Only the historical period surrounding the text
Only the readers personal emotional reaction
Close reading of the text on its own terms
Only the authors personal life and biography

quiz.q: Which elements does New Criticism typically focus on?
options: Only unrelated political events of the time
Only sales figures and popularity of the book
Structure, imagery, and language within the text itself
Only the publishers marketing strategy

quiz.q: What does New Criticism deliberately set aside when analyzing a text?
options: The imagery found in the writing
The authors biography and historical context
The words used within the text
The structure of the sentences

quiz.q: Why might a New Critic focus so closely on the words of a text itself?
options: Because words in a text have no connection to meaning
To understand meaning as something built directly within the language of the work
To avoid reading the text at all
Because close reading is considered unnecessary in literary study

quiz.q: New Criticism is often associated with a technique known as ___.
options: Only skimming a text quickly
Ignoring the text entirely
Reading only book reviews instead of the original text
Close reading

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Average Rate of Change Over an Interval
subjects.summary: Students calculate the average rate of change of a function over a given interval using the slope of the secant line, and interpret the result in context.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Average Rate of Change Over an Interval

quiz.q: The average rate of change of f over [a,b] is given by:
options: f(b) - f(a)
f(b)/f(a)

quiz.q: For f(x) = x², find the average rate of change over [1,3].
The average rate of change of a function over an interval corresponds geometrically to:
options: the slope of the secant line through the two endpoints
the maximum value on the interval
the y-intercept of the function
the slope of the tangent line at one endpoint

quiz.q: For f(x) = 2x³, find the average rate of change over [0,2].
A car travels 150 km in 3 hours. What is the average rate of change of distance with respect to time?
options: 3 km/h
150 km/h
450 km/h
50 km/h

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations: Solving Techniques
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: exponential equations can be solved by matching bases or applying logarithms to both sides, while logarithmic equations are often solved by rewriting them in exponential form.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations: Solving Techniques

quiz.q: What is one method for solving an exponential equation when both sides can be written with the same base?
options: Always assuming the answer is zero
Ignoring the exponents completely
Matching bases and setting the exponents equal
A concept unrelated to exponential equations

quiz.q: Solve for x: 2 to the power of x equals 8.
What is one common method for solving a logarithmic equation?
options: Rewriting it in exponential form
Ignoring the logarithm entirely
Always assuming x equals one
A concept unrelated to logarithmic equations

quiz.q: Why might applying a logarithm to both sides of an exponential equation be useful when the bases cannot easily be matched?
options: This concept has no connection to math
Applying a logarithm never helps solve an exponential equation
Logarithms allow the variable exponent to be brought down and solved using regular algebraic steps
Exponential equations can only ever be solved by guessing and checking

quiz.q: Why is checking a solution important after solving a logarithmic equation?
options: This concept has no connection to logarithms
Every possible numerical solution is always valid for a logarithmic equation
Logarithms are undefined for zero or negative values, so a solution must be checked to ensure it is valid
Solutions to logarithmic equations never need to be checked for validity

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Foucault Pendulum and Proof of Earths Rotation
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Foucault pendulum demonstrated Earths rotation by showing that its swinging plane appears to gradually rotate over time relative to the ground, providing direct physical evidence without needing to observe the stars.

quiz.q: What did the Foucault pendulum famously demonstrate?
options: Earths rotation
The speed of light
The existence of gravity
The structure of the atom

quiz.q: What is observed about the swinging plane of a Foucault pendulum over time?
options: It swings faster and faster with no explanation
It stops swinging entirely after a few minutes
It appears to gradually rotate relative to the ground
It remains perfectly fixed with no change at all

quiz.q: Why does the pendulums swinging plane appear to rotate?
options: The pendulum itself is designed to rotate on its own
The Earth is rotating beneath the pendulum, which maintains its plane of motion
The rotation is caused by wind resistance alone
The rotation is an optical illusion with no physical basis

quiz.q: What made the Foucault pendulum significant when first demonstrated?
options: It showed no connection to Earths motion
It could only be observed from outer space
It disproved that the Earth rotates at all
It provided direct physical evidence of Earths rotation without observing the stars

quiz.q: The rate at which a Foucault pendulums plane appears to rotate depends on ___.
options: The material the pendulum string is made of
The colour of the pendulum bob
The time of day only, with no other factor
The latitude at which the pendulum is located

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Reading: Analyzing the Doppelganger Motif in Literature
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Language strand: a doppelganger is a characters double or look-alike, often used as a literary motif to explore hidden identity, inner conflict, or a characters darker impulses within a story.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Reading: Analyzing the Doppelganger Motif in Literature

quiz.q: What is a doppelganger in literature?
options: A punctuation mark used in dialogue
A minor character who appears only once with no significance
A characters double or look-alike, often symbolizing a hidden side of that character
A type of formal citation used in essays

quiz.q: What theme does the doppelganger motif often explore?
options: A characters favourite hobbies with no deeper meaning
The exact geographic setting of a story
Hidden identity or inner conflict within a character
The history of a completely unrelated nation

quiz.q: Why might an author introduce a doppelganger for a main character?
options: To remove the main character from the story entirely
To eliminate the need for any character development
To confuse readers with no narrative purpose at all
To externalize a struggle happening within the characters own mind

quiz.q: A doppelganger is best described as a type of what literary device?
options: A formal citation format
A grammatical rule about sentence structure
A rhyme scheme used only in poetry
A recurring motif used to develop character and theme

quiz.q: How might a reader interpret the appearance of a doppelganger in a story?
options: As a signal that the story is exploring duality or conflicting aspects of identity
As proof that the story takes place in outer space
As an indication that the story has ended
As a sign that the story has no thematic content at all

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Instantaneous Rate of Change and the Difference Quotient
subjects.summary: Students estimate the instantaneous rate of change of a function at a point by evaluating the difference quotient for progressively smaller intervals, previewing the concept of a derivative.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Instantaneous Rate of Change and the Difference Quotient

quiz.q: The difference quotient for a function f is defined as:
options: [f(x) - f(x+h)] / h
[f(x+h) - f(x)] / h
f(x+h) - f(x)
[f(x+h) + f(x)] / h

quiz.q: The instantaneous rate of change at a point is estimated by taking the difference quotient and:
options: letting h approach 0
letting x approach 0
letting h approach infinity
setting h = 1

quiz.q: For f(x) = x², the simplified difference quotient [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h equals:
options: 2x
x + h
h
2x + h

quiz.q: For f(x) = x², what is the instantaneous rate of change at x = 3, found by letting h → 0 in 2x + h?
Why does the difference quotient approximate the instantaneous rate of change as h gets small?
options: The secant line through (x,f(x)) and (x+h,f(x+h)) approaches the tangent line at x as h → 0
h must equal zero to compute any rate
Smaller h always increases the function's value
Average and instantaneous rates are always exactly equal

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Related Rates: A Rotating Lighthouse Beam
subjects.summary: A lighthouse beam rotates at a constant number of revolutions per minute and sweeps across a straight shoreline. You'll convert the rotation rate to radians, then use a tangent relationship to find how fast the illuminated point moves along the shore.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Related Rates: A Rotating Lighthouse Beam

quiz.q: A lighthouse beam rotates at 4 revolutions per minute. Converting to radians per minute (1 revolution = 2π radians), what is dθ/dt?
options: 4π rad/min (about 12.57 rad/min)
8π rad/min (about 25.13 rad/min)
1440 rad/min (this is actually degrees per minute, not radians)
2/π rad/min (about 0.637 rad/min)

quiz.q: The lighthouse sits 200 m from a straight shoreline. Let θ be the angle between the beam and the perpendicular to the shore, and x be the distance along the shore from the closest point to the illuminated spot. Which relationship is correct?
options: x = 200 tanθ
x = 200 cosθ
x = 200/tanθ
x = 200 sinθ

quiz.q: Differentiating x = 200 tanθ with respect to time t gives which equation?
options: dx/dt = -200 sec^2θ (dθ/dt)
dx/dt = 200 tanθ (dθ/dt)
dx/dt = 200 sec^2θ (dθ/dt)
dx/dt = 200 sec^2θ

quiz.q: Using dθ/dt = 8π rad/min, how fast is the illuminated point moving along the shore at the instant θ = π/4 (where sec^2θ = 2)?
options: 400π m/min (about 1257 m/min)
3200π m/min (about 10053 m/min)
1600 m/min (this forgets to convert 4 rev/min into radians first)
1600π m/min (about 5027 m/min)

quiz.q: If the lighthouse were instead 400 m from the shore (double the distance) but rotated at the same angular rate, what would happen to dx/dt at the same angle θ = π/4?
options: It would quadruple, since dx/dt is proportional to d^2
It would stay the same, since the distance to shore doesn't affect dx/dt
It would be cut in half
It would double, since dx/dt = d·sec^2θ·(dθ/dt) is directly proportional to the perpendicular distance d

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Cavendish Experiment and Measuring the Gravitational Constant
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Cavendish experiment used a sensitive torsion balance to measure the tiny gravitational attraction between lead spheres, allowing the first accurate determination of the gravitational constant, G.

quiz.q: What device did the Cavendish experiment use to measure gravitational attraction?
options: A voltmeter
A simple spring scale
A telescope
A torsion balance

quiz.q: What force was the Cavendish experiment designed to measure?
options: The frictional force between two surfaces
The electric force between two charges
The magnetic force between two magnets
The gravitational attraction between two masses

quiz.q: What important physical constant did the Cavendish experiment help determine?
options: The gravitational constant, G
The mass of a proton
The speed of light
The charge of an electron

quiz.q: Why was measuring gravitational attraction between everyday objects considered so challenging?
options: The experiment required no precision instruments whatsoever
Gravity between small objects is actually very strong and easy to measure
Gravitational forces between small masses are extremely weak
Gravitational force has no measurable effect at all

quiz.q: The results of the Cavendish experiment allowed scientists to later calculate what other important quantity?
options: The temperature of the sun
The speed of sound
The mass of the Earth
The age of the universe

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Poetry: Prosody and Meter — The Music of Verse
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: prosody is the study of the rhythmic and sonic qualities of poetry, including meter, the patterned arrangement of stressed and unstressed syllables that gives a poem its underlying musical structure.

quiz.q: What does prosody study in poetry?
options: Only the punctuation used in a poem
Only the historical context of a poem
The rhythmic and sonic qualities of verse
Only the plot of a poem

quiz.q: What is meter in poetry?
options: The total number of words in a poem
A citation style used in essays
The patterned arrangement of stressed and unstressed syllables
A type of poem with no rhythm at all

quiz.q: What effect does meter give to a poem?
options: It only affects the poems visual appearance on a page
It has no effect on how the poem sounds
An underlying musical or rhythmic structure
It removes any sense of rhythm entirely

quiz.q: Which term describes a common meter pattern consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable?
options: Numeric
Iambic
Alphabetic
Chromatic

quiz.q: Why might a poet deliberately vary the meter within a poem?
options: Variation in meter always ruins a poems meaning entirely
Meter has no relationship to tone or meaning
To create emphasis or reflect a shift in tone or meaning
Meter can never be varied within a single poem

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Composition of Functions
subjects.summary: Students form and evaluate composite functions f(g(x)) and g(f(x)), and determine the domain of the resulting composite function.

quiz.q: If f(x) = x+2 and g(x) = x², find f(g(3)).
If f(x) = x+2 and g(x) = x², find g(f(3)).
If f(x) = √x and g(x) = x-4, find (f∘g)(x).
What is the domain of (f∘g)(x) = √(x-4) from the previous question?
options: all real numbers

quiz.q: Is f(g(x)) always equal to g(f(x)) for arbitrary functions f and g?
options: No, function composition is generally not commutative
Only for linear functions
Yes, always
Only for quadratic functions

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Analytic Geometry: Introduction to Conic Sections (Ellipses and Hyperbolas)
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: conic sections are curves formed by slicing a cone, including circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas, each with a distinct equation and shape.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Analytic Geometry: Introduction to Conic Sections (Ellipses and Hyperbolas)

quiz.q: What are conic sections?
options: Only straight lines drawn on a graph
A type of algebraic expression with no geometric meaning
A concept unrelated to geometry
Curves formed by slicing a cone, including circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas

quiz.q: What shape does an ellipse resemble?
options: A stretched or squashed circle
A concept unrelated to conic sections
A single straight line
Two separate curves opening away from each other

quiz.q: Does a hyperbola consist of two separate curves opening in opposite directions?
options: No, a hyperbola is always a single closed curve
Yes
A hyperbola is identical in shape to a circle
A concept unrelated to hyperbolas

quiz.q: Why is it useful to recognize which conic section an equation represents before graphing it?
options: This concept has no connection to math
Identifying the conic type reveals its general shape and key features, making an accurate sketch much easier
All conic sections are graphed using the exact same method regardless of type
The type of conic section never affects how an equation should be graphed

quiz.q: Why do engineers and astronomers find ellipses and hyperbolas useful for modelling real-world phenomena, such as planetary orbits?
options: These curves accurately describe many natural paths and shapes, including the elliptical orbits of planets
Ellipses and hyperbolas have no real-world applications outside of pure mathematics
This concept has no relevance to geometry
Planetary orbits are always perfectly circular, never elliptical

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Hall Effect
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Hall effect occurs when a magnetic field applied perpendicular to a current-carrying conductor produces a measurable voltage across the conductor, useful for determining charge carrier type and concentration.

quiz.q: What causes the Hall effect?
options: A magnetic field applied perpendicular to a current-carrying conductor
Sound waves passing through a solid
Heat applied to a conductor with no magnetic field
Light shining directly on a conductor

quiz.q: What is produced across the conductor in the Hall effect?
options: A measurable voltage, called the Hall voltage
A measurable change in temperature only
A measurable change in mass
A measurable change in colour

quiz.q: What can the Hall effect help scientists determine about a material?
options: The type and concentration of charge carriers
The taste of the material
The material weight in a vacuum
The exact age of the material

quiz.q: In what direction is the magnetic field applied relative to the current in the Hall effect?
options: The direction has no effect on the outcome
Perpendicular to the current
Parallel to the current
In the exact opposite direction of the current

quiz.q: The Hall effect has practical applications in devices such as ___.
options: Only devices with no electrical components
Only devices that measure sound
Only devices that measure taste
Sensors that measure magnetic fields

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literature: The Sublime in Romantic Literature
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: the sublime describes an overwhelming sense of awe, vastness, or terror often evoked by nature in Romantic literature, blending beauty with a feeling that exceeds ordinary human comprehension.

quiz.q: What does the sublime describe in Romantic literature?
options: A calm, ordinary, everyday feeling
A purely comedic tone in a text
An overwhelming sense of awe, vastness, or terror
A strictly mathematical concept

quiz.q: What natural settings commonly evoke the sublime in Romantic writing?
options: Vast mountains, storms, and other overwhelming landscapes
Only small, quiet gardens
Only urban city streets
Only indoor domestic settings

quiz.q: How does the sublime differ from simple beauty in Romantic aesthetics?
options: The sublime has no connection to emotion at all
The sublime combines beauty with an overwhelming or even terrifying vastness
The sublime refers only to small, delicate objects
The sublime is identical to simple beauty with no distinction

quiz.q: Why might Romantic writers be drawn to depicting the sublime?
options: To focus exclusively on mundane, everyday events
To avoid any emotional content in their writing
The sublime was never a concern for Romantic writers
To express emotions and experiences that exceed ordinary human comprehension

quiz.q: The concept of the sublime is often associated with which broader literary and philosophical movement?
options: Realism
Naturalism
Modernism
Romanticism

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Inverse Functions: Finding and Graphing f⁻¹(x)

subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Inverse Functions: Finding and Graphing f⁻¹(x)

quiz.q: The graph of f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of the graph of f(x) in the line:
options: y = x
y = -x

quiz.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = 2x + 6.
For a function's inverse to also be a function, f must be:
options: one-to-one (pass the horizontal line test)
even
increasing everywhere and nothing else
continuous only

quiz.q: If f(3) = 7, what is f⁻¹(7)?
Find the inverse of f(x) = x³ + 1.

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Trigonometry: Sum and Difference Identities
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: sum and difference identities express trigonometric functions of the sum or difference of two angles, such as sin(A+B) equals sin(A)cos(B) plus cos(A)sin(B), in terms of the original angles.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Trigonometry: Sum and Difference Identities

quiz.q: What do sum and difference identities express?
options: Only the value of a single angle
A concept unrelated to trigonometry
Trigonometric functions of the sum or difference of two angles
The area of a triangle

quiz.q: What is the identity for sin(A+B)?
options: sin(A)cos(B) + cos(A)sin(B)
sin(A)cos(B) - cos(A)sin(B)
sin(A) + sin(B)
cos(A)cos(B) - sin(A)sin(B)

quiz.q: Can sum and difference identities help evaluate the exact trigonometric value of an angle like 75 degrees, using 45 and 30 degrees?
options: A concept unrelated to sum and difference identities
Yes
Only a calculator can ever find such a value, with no formula available
No, sum and difference identities never help evaluate exact trigonometric values

quiz.q: Why are sum and difference identities useful when a trigonometric equation involves an angle that is not a common reference angle?
options: These identities never help simplify equations involving uncommon angles
They allow an uncommon angle to be rewritten as a sum or difference of angles with known exact trigonometric values
This concept has no connection to math
Every angle already has a memorized exact trigonometric value without needing any identity

quiz.q: Why are sum and difference identities considered a foundation for deriving other identities, such as the double-angle formulas?
options: Double-angle formulas were developed with no connection to any other identity
Sum and difference identities have no mathematical connection to double-angle formulas
This concept has no relevance to trigonometry
Setting the two angles equal to each other in a sum identity directly produces the corresponding double-angle formula

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: The Coriolis Effect
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Coriolis effect is an apparent deflection of moving objects observed in a rotating reference frame, such as Earth, causing winds and ocean currents to curve rather than travel in perfectly straight paths.

quiz.q: What is the Coriolis effect?
options: An apparent deflection of moving objects in a rotating reference frame
A type of magnetic field around Earth
A change in an objects mass due to motion
A force that only exists in outer space

quiz.q: What causes the Coriolis effect on Earth?
options: Ocean temperature changes only
Earths gravitational pull alone
Earths rotation
Solar radiation striking the Earths surface

quiz.q: How does the Coriolis effect influence wind and ocean currents?
options: It has no influence on wind or ocean currents at all
It only affects currents in a single, fixed direction everywhere
It causes them to curve rather than travel in perfectly straight paths
It causes them to instantly stop moving

quiz.q: In which hemisphere does the Coriolis effect typically deflect moving objects to the right of their motion?
options: The Northern Hemisphere
Only at the equator, with no deflection elsewhere
Neither hemisphere experiences any deflection
The Southern Hemisphere

quiz.q: The Coriolis effect is an example of a ___ force, observed only within a rotating frame of reference.
options: Purely nuclear
Fictitious (or apparent)
Purely gravitational
Purely magnetic

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literature: The Artist Novel and the Kunstlerroman
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a Kunstlerroman, or artist novel, is a type of coming-of-age narrative that follows the development of an artist, writer, or musician from youth into creative maturity, closely related to the broader bildungsroman tradition.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Literature: The Artist Novel and the Kunstlerroman

quiz.q: What is a Kunstlerroman?
options: A coming-of-age narrative that follows the development of an artist from youth into creative maturity
A short poem with a strict rhyme scheme
A formal legal document used in court proceedings
A type of scientific research paper

quiz.q: What broader narrative tradition is the Kunstlerroman closely related to?
options: The detective procedural
The bildungsroman
The captivity narrative
The epistolary novel

quiz.q: What type of protagonist does a Kunstlerroman typically follow?
options: A retired judge with no creative pursuits
A historical military general
An anonymous crowd with no individual characters
An artist, writer, or musician

quiz.q: What does a Kunstlerroman typically trace across its plot?
options: The construction of a large public building
The growth of the protagonists creative identity and craft
The history of a nations legal system
The migration patterns of a species of bird

quiz.q: Why might an author choose the Kunstlerroman form?
options: To focus exclusively on unrelated historical events
To avoid describing any character development at all
To eliminate any reference to art or creativity
To explore how artistic vision and personal identity develop together over time

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Combining Functions: Graphing Sums and Products

add the x-values of f and g
average the y-values of f and g at that x
add the y-values of f and g at that x

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Probability: The Binomial Probability Distribution
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: a binomial probability distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success, such as repeated coin flips.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Probability: The Binomial Probability Distribution

quiz.q: What does a binomial probability distribution model?
options: A relationship between two unrelated variables
The average of a single continuous measurement
A concept unrelated to probability
The number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials

quiz.q: In a binomial setting, must each trial have the same probability of success?
options: No, each trial’s probability of success is always different
Probability of success never applies to a binomial trial
Yes
A concept unrelated to binomial distributions

quiz.q: Which of these is a classic example of a binomial experiment?
options: Flipping a fair coin 10 times and counting the number of heads
A concept unrelated to binomial distributions
Measuring the exact height of every student in a class
Recording the colour of a single object one time only

quiz.q: Why must the trials in a binomial distribution be independent of one another?
options: Independence ensures the outcome of one trial does not change the probability of success on another trial, keeping the model accurate
This concept has no connection to math
Independence between trials has no effect on whether a binomial model applies

quiz.q: Why is the binomial distribution useful for quality control, such as estimating the number of defective items in a batch?
options: The binomial distribution has no application to quality control processes
This concept has no relevance to probability
Defect rates can never be modelled using any probability distribution

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: Brownian Motion and Einsteins Explanation
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: Brownian motion is the random, erratic movement of small particles suspended in a fluid, and Einsteins 1905 explanation showed that this motion results from countless collisions with fast-moving molecules, providing strong evidence for the existence of atoms.

quiz.q: What is Brownian motion?
options: The random, erratic movement of small particles suspended in a fluid
A type of motion found only in solids
A steady, predictable motion in a straight line
A motion that occurs only in a vacuum

quiz.q: What did Einstein propose as the cause of Brownian motion in 1905?
options: Sound waves pushing the particles around
A hidden magnetic field acting on the particles
Gravity alone, with no molecular involvement
Countless collisions with fast-moving molecules in the fluid

quiz.q: Why was Einsteins explanation of Brownian motion scientifically significant?
options: It had no connection to atomic theory
It showed that fluids contain no moving particles at all
It provided strong evidence for the existence of atoms and molecules
It disproved the existence of atoms entirely

quiz.q: What type of particles is Brownian motion typically observed in?
options: Small particles suspended in a liquid or gas
Only extremely large, heavy objects
Only particles found in outer space
Only particles frozen in solid ice

quiz.q: Brownian motion helped confirm which broader scientific theory?
options: The kinetic theory of matter
The theory of continental drift
The theory of electromagnetism
The theory of general relativity

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literary Theory: Biographical Criticism — Reading the Author into the Text
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: biographical criticism interprets a literary work by examining connections between the text and the authors life experiences, beliefs, and historical circumstances, while remaining cautious about reducing a text entirely to biography.

quiz.q: What does biographical criticism examine when interpreting a text?
options: Connections between the text and the authors life experiences
Only unrelated events from a different century
Only the readers personal opinions with no textual evidence
Only the physical appearance of the printed book

quiz.q: What might a biographical critic explore about an author?
options: Only their handwriting style
Only their favourite colour
Only their taste in food
Their beliefs and historical circumstances

quiz.q: What caution do scholars often raise about biographical criticism?
options: The risk of reducing a text entirely to the authors biography, ignoring other interpretations
That biographical criticism should replace all close reading of a text
That an authors life never has any relevance to their work
That biography should always be the only valid approach to a text

quiz.q: Why might knowing an authors historical circumstances be useful when reading their work?
options: It replaces the need to read the text at all
It can provide context that deepens understanding of the texts themes or choices
Historical context is always completely irrelevant to a text
It guarantees a single, definitive interpretation of every text

quiz.q: Biographical criticism is often used alongside other approaches, such as ___.
options: Only analysis of unrelated scientific data
Only mathematical analysis, with no literary connection
No other critical approaches are ever combined with it
Historical or formalist analysis, to build a fuller picture of a text

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions

subjects.summary: Students determine the domain of sum, product, quotient, and composite functions by considering the domains of the original functions and any new restrictions introduced, such as division by zero.

quiz.q: The domain of (f+g)(x) is generally:
options: always all real numbers
the union of the domains of f and g
the intersection of the domains of f and g
the domain of f only

options: f(x) = g(x)
