subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: The Secant Method for Root Approximation
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Calculus strand: the secant method approximates a root of a function by drawing a line through two nearby points on the curve and using the x-intercept of that line as the next approximation, avoiding the need for a derivative required by Newtons method.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 12 Calculus and Vectors

quiz.q: What line does the secant method use to generate its next root approximation?
options: A vertical line through a single point
A line tangent to the curve at one point only
A line through two nearby points on the curve
A line with no relationship to the curve

quiz.q: What advantage does the secant method have over Newtons method?
options: It always converges faster than every other method
It does not require computing a derivative of the function
It guarantees an exact answer after a single step
It requires exactly one initial guess rather than two

quiz.q: What quantity from the secant line gives the next root approximation?
options: The midpoint of the two original points
Its x-intercept
Its slope alone, with no intercept used
Its y-intercept

quiz.q: How many previous approximations does the secant method use to generate the next one?
options: One
Zero
Two
An unlimited number, all at once

quiz.q: How does the secant method generally compare to the bisection method studied earlier in terms of convergence speed?
options: It generally converges faster than bisection, though convergence is not guaranteed
Bisection converges without ever needing two initial points
The two methods have identical convergence behaviour in every case
It always converges more slowly than bisection

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Total Internal Reflection and Fiber-Optic Communication
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: total internal reflection occurs when light travelling in a denser medium strikes a boundary with a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle, reflecting entirely back into the denser medium, a principle exploited by fiber-optic cables to transmit light signals with minimal loss.

quiz.q: What is total internal reflection?
options: A phenomenon that only occurs with sound waves
The complete absorption of light at any surface
Light passing completely unaffected through any boundary
Light reflecting entirely back into a denser medium when it strikes a boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle

quiz.q: What condition on the angle of incidence causes total internal reflection to occur?
options: The angle must be measured from a less dense to a denser medium
The angle of incidence must be exactly zero degrees
The angle of incidence has no effect on the outcome
The angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle

quiz.q: What technology exploits total internal reflection to transmit signals over long distances?
options: A device with no connection to light at all
Fiber-optic cables
A simple glass window with no coating
Ordinary copper telephone wire

quiz.q: Why must light travel from a denser to a less dense medium for total internal reflection to be possible?
options: A critical angle, beyond which total internal reflection occurs, exists only when moving toward a lower refractive index
Refractive index has no role in this phenomenon
Light must first stop moving entirely for reflection to occur
Total internal reflection occurs equally in every direction of travel

quiz.q: What advantage does fiber-optic transmission gain from total internal reflection?
options: The signal is destroyed at every bend in the fiber
The fiber must be perfectly straight with no curves allowed
The light signal is transmitted with minimal loss along the length of the fiber
The signal converts entirely into sound during transmission

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literary Naturalism: Determinism and the Novel
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: literary naturalism extends realism by portraying characters as shaped largely by heredity, environment, and social forces beyond their control, presenting human behaviour with a scientific, often pessimistic determinism associated with writers such as Emile Zola.

quiz.q: What forces do naturalist novels typically emphasize as shaping character?
options: Heredity, environment, and social forces beyond the characters control
Only the characters own free choices, with no outside influence
Supernatural forces such as ghosts and spirits
Pure random chance with no underlying pattern at all

quiz.q: How does literary naturalism extend the realism studied in earlier literary traditions?
options: It focuses exclusively on fantastical, magical events
It rejects any connection to observable human behaviour
It removes all realistic detail from the narrative entirely
It adds a scientific, deterministic view of human behaviour beyond typical realistic detail

quiz.q: What tone often characterizes naturalist fiction?
options: An unrelentingly cheerful, optimistic outlook
A tone with no emotional quality whatsoever
A pessimistic determinism
A tone of pure comic absurdity throughout

quiz.q: Which nineteenth-century writer is closely associated with literary naturalism?
options: William Wordsworth
Jonathan Swift
Geoffrey Chaucer
Emile Zola

quiz.q: How does determinism in naturalist fiction typically affect a characters sense of agency?
options: Naturalist characters are entirely free of environmental influence
Characters have complete, unlimited control over every outcome
Characters have limited control, being largely shaped by forces beyond them
Agency plays no role in naturalist fiction at all

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Discrete Math: Boolean Algebra and Logic Gates
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: Boolean algebra manipulates true and false values using operations such as AND, OR, and NOT, providing the mathematical foundation for logic gates and digital circuits that underlie modern computing.

quiz.q: What values does Boolean algebra fundamentally operate on?
options: Complex numbers exclusively
Negative fractions only
True and false (or one and zero) values
Only irrational numbers

quiz.q: Which three operations form the basic building blocks of Boolean algebra?
options: AND, OR, and NOT
Sine, cosine, and tangent
Addition, subtraction, and multiplication
Integration, differentiation, and limits

quiz.q: What physical devices implement Boolean operations inside a computer?
options: Ordinary resistors with no logical function
Mechanical gears with no electrical component
Simple wires with no components
Logic gates

quiz.q: What does the AND operation output when both of its inputs are true?
options: A value that is neither true nor false
False
True
An undefined result

quiz.q: Why is Boolean algebra considered foundational to modern computing?
options: It only applies to purely abstract, unused mathematics
It has no connection to computers or digital devices
It was replaced entirely by a different number system in modern computers
It underlies the design of digital circuits and the logic gates used inside computers

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Calculus Preview: An Introduction to Limits
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Math strand: a limit describes the value a function approaches as its input gets closer to a specific point, forming the conceptual foundation for derivatives and the broader study of calculus.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Calculus Preview: An Introduction to Limits

quiz.q: What does a limit describe?
options: The exact maximum value of any function
The value a function approaches as its input gets closer to a specific point
A fixed number that never changes across all functions
The total area under every curve

quiz.q: What foundational concept in calculus relies on the idea of a limit?
options: Long division only
Simple counting
The derivative
Basic addition

quiz.q: Can a function have a limit at a point even if it is undefined at that exact point?
options: Yes, a limit can exist even if the function itself is undefined there
Limits are unrelated to whether a function is defined
A function can never have any limit under any circumstance
No, a limit only exists if the function is defined at that exact point

quiz.q: As x approaches 2, what does the limit of the function f(x)=x+1 approach?
Why do mathematicians consider limits a foundational concept in calculus?
options: They eliminate the need to study functions entirely
They only apply to whole numbers with no fractions
They provide a precise way to describe behaviour near a point without requiring the function be defined there
They have no connection to any other calculus concept

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Newtons Rings and Thin-Film Interference
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: Newtons rings are a pattern of concentric bright and dark circular fringes produced by the interference of light reflected between a curved lens surface and a flat plate, arising from the varying thickness of the thin air film trapped between them.

quiz.q: What pattern do Newtons rings form?
options: Concentric bright and dark circular fringes
A uniform, unchanging field of one colour
A random, non-repeating scatter of colour
A single straight bright line with no pattern

quiz.q: What produces the interference pattern seen in Newtons rings?
options: A magnetic field acting directly on light
Light passing through a completely opaque solid block
Sound waves reflecting off a curved surface
Light reflected between a curved lens surface and a flat plate, with a varying air-film thickness between them

quiz.q: What varies across the trapped air film to produce the ring pattern?
options: Its colour, independent of any physical property
Its electric charge
Its temperature alone, with no thickness variation
Its thickness

quiz.q: What broader wave phenomenon explains the formation of Newtons rings?
options: The photoelectric effect
Nuclear decay
Thin-film interference
Simple reflection with no interference involved

quiz.q: Why do Newtons rings appear circular rather than in some other shape?
options: The rings are drawn intentionally with no physical cause
The air-film thickness varies symmetrically around the point of contact of the curved lens
Circular shapes are the only shapes light can ever form
The flat plate is always perfectly circular in shape

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Memoir and the Art of Life Writing
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: memoir is a nonfiction form of life writing that reconstructs a specific period or theme from the authors own life, shaping remembered experience into narrative through selection, reflection, and a controlling perspective distinct from a comprehensive autobiography.

quiz.q: What does memoir typically reconstruct?
options: A specific period or theme from the authors own life
A biography of a person the author has never met
A complete, chronological record of an entire life from birth to the present
A purely fictional life invented for entertainment

quiz.q: How does memoir differ from a comprehensive autobiography?
options: It is always written by someone other than the subject
It focuses on a selected period or theme rather than the whole of a life
It cannot include any reflection or interpretation
It must always cover every year of the authors life in equal detail

quiz.q: What shapes remembered experience into a coherent narrative in memoir?
options: Pure, unfiltered transcription with no shaping at all
A total absence of any narrative structure
Random, disconnected fragments with no unifying thread
Selection, reflection, and a controlling perspective

quiz.q: To which broader genre category does memoir belong?
options: Pure fantasy fiction
Nonfiction life writing
Formal scientific reporting
Dramatic verse composed for the stage

quiz.q: Why might a memoirist rely on a controlling perspective when shaping their material?
options: Because memoir requires no interpretation of events
To avoid including any personal experience whatsoever
Because a controlling perspective is forbidden in nonfiction
To shape scattered memory into a coherent, meaningful narrative

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Statistics: Correlation and the Pearson Correlation Coefficient
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: the Pearson correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two quantitative variables, producing a value between negative one and positive one that indicates how closely the data follow a straight line.

quiz.q: What does the Pearson correlation coefficient measure?
options: The total number of data points collected
The strength and direction of the linear relationship between two quantitative variables
The exact mean of a single data set
The mode of a categorical variable

quiz.q: What range of values can the Pearson correlation coefficient take?
options: Any real number with no upper or lower bound
From zero to positive one hundred
From negative one to positive one
Only the values zero and one

quiz.q: What does a Pearson correlation coefficient close to zero indicate?
options: Little to no linear relationship between the two variables
A perfect negative linear relationship
A perfect positive linear relationship
That the two variables are identical

quiz.q: What does a Pearson correlation coefficient of positive one indicate?
options: A perfect positive linear relationship between the two variables
An undefined relationship
No relationship of any kind
A perfect negative linear relationship

quiz.q: Why is correlation not the same as causation, an important caution when interpreting a Pearson coefficient?
options: Causation can never be studied using correlation at all
Correlation and causation are mathematically identical concepts
A strong correlation always proves direct causation
A strong correlation does not necessarily mean one variable causes changes in the other

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Math Review: Advanced Algebra, Number Theory, and Calculus Preview
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Math strand review: students revisit synthetic division, prime factorization, the Pythagorean trigonometric identity, three-variable systems, the dot product, mathematical induction, insurance and risk, conditional probability, and limits.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Math Review: Advanced Algebra, Number Theory, and Calculus Preview

quiz.q: What does synthetic division provide a shortcut for?
options: Finding the area of a triangle
Solving a system of linear equations
Dividing a polynomial by a linear binomial of the form x-a
Multiplying two polynomials together

quiz.q: What does the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic state?
options: Every integer has infinitely many different prime factorizations
Every integer greater than one has exactly one prime factorization, aside from order
Only even numbers can be factored into primes
Prime numbers do not exist

quiz.q: What does the Pythagorean trigonometric identity state?
options: Sine plus cosine always equals zero
Sine minus cosine always equals one
Tangent squared always equals negative one
Sine squared plus cosine squared of an angle equals one

quiz.q: What type of value does the dot product of two vectors produce?
options: A new vector with a different direction
A complex number
A matrix
A single scalar value

quiz.q: What does a limit describe?
options: The total area under every curve
The exact maximum value of any function
A fixed number that never changes across all functions
The value a function approaches as its input gets closer to a specific point

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: The Tyndall Effect and Light Scattering in Colloids
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by particles suspended in a colloid, making a beam of light passing through the mixture visible from the side, distinguished from Rayleigh scattering by the larger size of the scattering particles relative to atmospheric molecules.

quiz.q: What is the Tyndall effect?
options: The scattering of light by particles suspended in a colloid, making a beam of light visible from the side
The complete absorption of all light by a transparent solution
A phenomenon that only occurs in a perfect vacuum
The bending of light as it passes through a single flat pane of glass

quiz.q: What makes a light beam visible when it passes through a colloid?
options: Light scattered sideways by particles suspended in the mixture
A chemical reaction that produces new light
The beam gaining additional energy from the colloid
The complete absence of any particles in the mixture

quiz.q: How does the Tyndall effect differ from the Rayleigh scattering studied earlier in this course?
options: It involves larger particles than the molecules responsible for Rayleigh scattering
It occurs only in a perfect vacuum, unlike Rayleigh scattering
It involves no particles of any kind
The two phenomena are identical in every respect

quiz.q: Which everyday scene commonly demonstrates the Tyndall effect?
options: A perfectly clear glass of water with no visible beam
A completely opaque solid block with no light passing through
A beam of light travelling through total darkness with no scattering
A visible beam of light shining through fog or a dusty room

quiz.q: Why can the Tyndall effect be used to distinguish a colloid from a true solution?
options: Colloidal particles scatter light visibly, while the much smaller particles in a true solution generally do not
True solutions always scatter light more strongly than colloids
Colloids and true solutions scatter light in exactly the same way
Neither colloids nor true solutions can scatter light at all

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: The Ballad Tradition: Narrative Song and Folk Verse
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: the ballad is a narrative folk poem originally meant to be sung, typically composed in quatrains with a simple rhyme scheme, recounting a dramatic story of love, tragedy, or adventure through compressed, often repetitive language.

quiz.q: What is a ballad in its traditional form?
options: A purely visual poem with no words at all
A prose essay with no narrative elements
A narrative folk poem originally meant to be sung
A formal legal document with no poetic content

quiz.q: What stanza form do ballads typically use?
options: Stanzas with no consistent line count at all
A single unbroken line with no stanza breaks
Fourteen-line stanzas with an intricate rhyme scheme
Quatrains with a simple rhyme scheme

quiz.q: What kinds of stories do ballads commonly recount?
options: Dramatic stories of love, tragedy, or adventure
Purely abstract mathematical concepts
Detailed technical instructions for a craft
A list of unrelated historical dates

quiz.q: What stylistic feature often marks ballad language?
options: Compressed, often repetitive language, including refrains
Language borrowed entirely from formal legal writing
A total absence of rhythm or musicality
Extremely long, unbroken sentences with no repetition

quiz.q: How does the ballads oral, musical origin shape its form?
options: It favours memorable rhythm, repetition, and simple structure suited to singing
It has no influence on the poems structure at all
It requires the poem to be read silently and never performed
It requires the poem to be entirely unrhymed and unmetered

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Discrete Math: Combinatorial Game Theory and the Game of Nim
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: combinatorial game theory analyzes two-player games of perfect information with no chance element, and the game of Nim, in which players remove objects from piles, provides a classic example whose winning strategy is determined using the binary XOR of pile sizes.

quiz.q: What kind of games does combinatorial game theory study?
options: Games with an unlimited number of players and no defined rules
Games decided purely by rolling dice with no strategy involved
Games where information is always hidden from both players
Two-player games of perfect information with no chance element

quiz.q: What is the basic action taken by players in the game of Nim?
options: Rolling a die to determine the next move
Removing objects from piles
Placing new objects onto an empty board
Drawing cards from a shuffled deck

quiz.q: What operation determines the winning strategy in the game of Nim?
options: A simple sum of the pile sizes with no further calculation
The largest pile size alone, with no other calculation
The binary XOR of the pile sizes
A random guess with no calculation involved

quiz.q: What does it mean for a game to have perfect information?
options: Neither player has any knowledge of the game at all
Both players can see the entire state of the game at all times
Only one player can ever see the game state
The game state changes randomly with no visibility

quiz.q: Why is Nim considered a classic example within combinatorial game theory?
options: It has never been solved and remains a complete mystery
It cannot be analyzed mathematically in any way
It has a fully solved, elegant winning strategy that illustrates the fields core ideas
It involves no strategy of any kind

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: The Scalar Triple Product and the Volume of a Parallelepiped
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Calculus and Vectors strand: the scalar triple product combines three vectors using a cross product and a dot product to produce a single number whose absolute value equals the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 12 Calculus and Vectors

quiz.q: What operations combine to form the scalar triple product?
options: A single addition of three vectors with no multiplication
Two separate dot products with no cross product
Division of one vector by another
A cross product followed by a dot product

quiz.q: What geometric quantity does the absolute value of the scalar triple product equal?
options: The area of a triangle formed by two of the vectors
The length of a single vector alone
The volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors
The angle between two of the vectors

quiz.q: How many vectors are combined to form a scalar triple product?
options: One
Three
Four
Two

quiz.q: What does a scalar triple product of zero indicate about the three vectors involved?
options: The vectors must all have zero magnitude
The vectors are coplanar, meaning they are linearly dependent
The vectors have no defined direction at all
The vectors are mutually perpendicular with maximum volume

quiz.q: How does the scalar triple product build on the cross product studied earlier in this course?
options: It requires computing four separate cross products
It replaces the cross product with simple scalar multiplication
It uses the cross product of two vectors, then takes the dot product of that result with the third vector
It has no relationship to the cross product whatsoever

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Biology: Photosynthesis in Depth: Light and Dark Reactions
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: photosynthesis consists of two stages, the light-dependent reactions that capture solar energy, and the light-independent (dark) reactions that use that energy to build sugars.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Biology: Photosynthesis in Depth: Light and Dark Reactions

quiz.q: How many main stages does photosynthesis consist of?
options: One
Two
Five
A concept unrelated to biology

quiz.q: What do the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis capture?
options: Solar energy
Nothing at all related to energy
A concept unrelated to photosynthesis
Only carbon dioxide from the air

quiz.q: Do the light-independent, or dark, reactions use energy captured earlier to build sugars?
options: A concept unrelated to photosynthesis
Sugars are never produced during photosynthesis
Yes
No, the dark reactions never use any captured energy

quiz.q: Why are the light-independent reactions sometimes called dark reactions, even though they can occur during the day?
options: The dark reactions only ever occur at night, never during the day
This concept has no connection to photosynthesis
Dark reactions require intense direct sunlight at all times
They do not directly require light, unlike the light-dependent reactions

quiz.q: Why is understanding both stages of photosynthesis important for understanding plant growth?
options: The two stages of photosynthesis have no connection to how plants grow
Only one of the two stages actually contributes to a plant’s growth
This concept has no relevance to biology
Both stages work together to convert light energy into the chemical energy plants use to grow

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Concrete Poetry: Shape and Typography as Meaning
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: concrete poetry arranges words, letters, and typography on the page so that the visual shape of the poem itself contributes directly to its meaning, treating the poems physical layout as inseparable from its verbal content.

quiz.q: What does concrete poetry emphasize alongside its words?
options: Only the sound of the words when read aloud, with no visual element
A complete absence of any typography or layout
A strict, unvarying rhyme scheme with no visual concerns
The visual shape and typographic arrangement of the poem on the page

quiz.q: How does the visual shape of a concrete poem typically relate to its meaning?
options: It always contradicts and undermines the poems stated subject
It has no connection to the poems meaning whatsoever
It exists purely by accident with no intended effect
It contributes directly to and reinforces the poems meaning

quiz.q: What is treated as inseparable from verbal content in concrete poetry?
options: The publishers logo on the page
The poems title alone, with no reference to the body text
The font size used in an unrelated document
The poems physical layout on the page

quiz.q: How does concrete poetry differ from a conventional lyric poem read primarily for its sound and sense?
options: It is identical in every respect to a conventional lyric poem
It rejects the use of words entirely
It also relies on visual, spatial arrangement as a source of meaning
It cannot be printed or displayed visually at all

quiz.q: Why might a poet arrange words into a visual shape to represent an abstract idea?
options: Abstract ideas cannot be represented through any visual arrangement
Visual form can mirror or enact the poems subject in ways plain text alone cannot
Typography has no effect on how a poem is interpreted
Visual form always obscures a poems meaning entirely

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Applications of Exponential Functions: Depreciation and Present Value
subjects.summary: Students apply exponential decay models to real-world depreciation of assets such as vehicles and equipment, and use exponential functions to calculate present value, distinguishing exponential depreciation from straight-line depreciation.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Applications of Exponential Functions: Depreciation and Present Value

quiz.q: A car purchased for $28,000 depreciates at 15% per year. Which function models its value V after t years?
Using V = 28000(0.85)^t, approximately what is the car's value after 4 years? (0.85^4 ≈ 0.522)
How does exponential depreciation differ from straight-line (linear) depreciation?
options: Linear depreciation can never reach zero value
They are mathematically identical
Exponential depreciation loses a fixed percentage of the current value each year, so the dollar amount lost decreases over time; linear loses a fixed dollar amount each year
Exponential depreciation loses the same dollar amount each year; linear loses a percentage

quiz.q: Present value P of an amount A to be received in t years, given an annual discount rate r, is modeled by which formula?
options: P = A - rt
P = A + rt
P = A(1 + r)^t

quiz.q: An investment will be worth $10,000 in 5 years. Using a discount rate of 6% per year, which expression gives its present value?

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Calculus: The Chain Rule for Derivatives
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the chain rule provides a method for differentiating a composite function, one function nested inside another, by multiplying the derivative of the outer function by the derivative of the inner function.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Calculus: The Chain Rule for Derivatives

quiz.q: What does the chain rule allow you to differentiate?
options: A composite function, one function nested inside another
Only whole numbers with no variables
Only a single constant term
Only a sum of two unrelated functions

quiz.q: How is the chain rule generally applied?
options: By ignoring the inner function entirely
By dividing the outer function by the inner function
By adding the two functions together first
By multiplying the derivative of the outer function by the derivative of the inner function

quiz.q: Which type of function most clearly requires the chain rule to differentiate?
options: A function with no inner expression at all
A single constant with no variable
A composite function such as the square of a trigonometric expression
A simple linear function like y equals x

quiz.q: The chain rule builds directly on which earlier differentiation rules?
options: Only basic arithmetic with no calculus involved
Only the quadratic formula
Only the Pythagorean Theorem
The power rule and the basic derivative rules

quiz.q: Why is the chain rule essential in calculus?
options: It eliminates the need for the power rule entirely
Many real functions are composite functions that cannot be differentiated with simpler rules alone
It replaces the need to ever find a derivative
It only applies to functions with no variables

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics: Torque and Rotational Equilibrium
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: torque measures the turning effect of a force around a pivot point, and an object is in rotational equilibrium when the net torque acting on it is zero.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Physics: Torque and Rotational Equilibrium

quiz.q: What does torque measure?
options: A concept unrelated to physics
The turning effect of a force around a pivot point
The temperature of an object
The total mass of an object

quiz.q: When is an object in rotational equilibrium?
options: When it is moving at a constant speed in a straight line
When the net torque acting on it is zero
When no force acts on it at all
A concept unrelated to torque

quiz.q: Does increasing the distance from the pivot point increase the torque produced by a given force?
options: No, distance from the pivot has no effect on torque
Torque only depends on the mass of an object
A concept unrelated to torque
Yes

quiz.q: Why might a longer wrench make it easier to loosen a tight bolt compared to a shorter one?
options: This concept has no connection to physics
Wrench length never has any effect on the torque applied to a bolt
A shorter wrench always produces more torque than a longer one
A longer wrench increases the distance from the pivot, producing greater torque for the same applied force

quiz.q: Why is understanding rotational equilibrium important when designing a seesaw or balance scale?
options: This concept has no relevance to physics
It helps ensure the torques on each side balance so the object remains stable and level
Rotational equilibrium has no connection to how a seesaw or balance scale works
Seesaws and balance scales never rely on any torque balance

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Weird Fiction and the Aesthetics of Cosmic Horror
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: weird fiction evokes a sense of cosmic horror by suggesting the existence of vast, indifferent, and unknowable forces beyond human comprehension, emphasizing dread and awe over conventional monsters or explainable threats.

quiz.q: What sense does weird fiction primarily aim to evoke in its readers?
options: Light comic relief with no sense of unease
A purely romantic, sentimental mood
Cosmic horror, or dread at vast, unknowable forces
A calm, reassuring sense of order and safety

quiz.q: What kind of forces does weird fiction typically suggest lie beyond human comprehension?
options: Forces that are always fully explained by the story
Forces limited strictly to ordinary human emotions
Small, easily understood household objects
Vast, indifferent, unknowable cosmic forces

quiz.q: What does weird fiction emphasize over a conventional, fully explainable monster?
options: A monster whose motives are entirely clear
A detailed scientific explanation for every event
Dread and awe at something fundamentally incomprehensible
A cheerful resolution with no lingering unease

quiz.q: How does weird fictions cosmic horror differ from a typical ghost story with a clearly resolved cause?
options: It contains no sense of fear or dread at all
It focuses entirely on realistic, everyday concerns
It emphasizes the incomprehensibility and indifference of the universe rather than offering a resolvable threat
It always provides a complete, tidy explanation for every event

quiz.q: Why might a writer of weird fiction leave the central threat vague or only partially explained?
options: Because fully explaining a threat always increases its horror
To preserve a sense of the unknowable that generates cosmic dread
Because vague threats are required by law in this genre
Because leaving details vague eliminates all sense of atmosphere

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Statistics: The Central Limit Theorem
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: the central limit theorem states that the distribution of sample means drawn from a population approaches a normal distribution as the sample size grows large, regardless of the shape of the original population distribution.

quiz.q: What does the central limit theorem describe?
options: The exact height of a single randomly chosen individual
The total sum of every value in an entire population
The distribution of sample means approaching a normal distribution as sample size grows large
A rule that applies only to perfectly normal populations

quiz.q: What happens to the sampling distribution of the mean as sample size increases, according to the theorem?
options: It becomes increasingly unpredictable with no pattern
It approaches a normal distribution
It shrinks to a single fixed point with no variation
It always becomes perfectly uniform

quiz.q: Does the central limit theorem require the original population to already be normally distributed?
options: The theorem does not apply to any real population
No, it holds regardless of the shape of the original population
Yes, it only applies when the population is already normal
Yes, and it fails completely for any other population shape

quiz.q: Why is the central limit theorem considered foundational to inferential statistics?
options: It proves that no statistical inference is ever possible
It only applies to a single specific data set with no generalization
It eliminates the need for any sampling at all
It justifies using normal-distribution-based methods for sample means even from non-normal populations

quiz.q: How does the central limit theorem connect to the normal distribution studied earlier in this course?
options: It replaces the normal distribution with the Poisson distribution entirely
It shows that sample means tend toward that same normal distribution as sample size grows
It has no connection to the normal distribution at all
It shows the normal distribution can never describe sample means

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Vectors: Work Done by a Force Along a Displacement
subjects.summary: Calculate the work done by a constant force acting through a displacement using the dot product formula W = F·d, including cases where force and displacement are given as vectors or as magnitude-and-angle pairs.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Vectors: Work Done by a Force Along a Displacement

quiz.q: A force F = (10, 5) N acts on an object as it moves through displacement d = (3, 4) m. Find the work done.
A constant force of magnitude 20 N acts at an angle of 60° to the direction of a 15 m displacement. Find the work done.
A force F = (8, −6) N is applied while an object undergoes displacement d = (−2, 5) m. Find the work done.
options: 5 J

quiz.q: A force acts on an object as it moves through displacement d = (6, 0) m. Which of the following forces does zero work on the object?
A worker pulls a sled with a force of 50 N directed at 40° above the horizontal, moving the sled 12 m horizontally. How much work does the force do?

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: The Rayleigh Criterion and the Resolving Power of Optical Instruments
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Rayleigh criterion defines the minimum angular separation at which two point sources can be distinguished as separate by an optical instrument, based on the diffraction pattern produced by the instruments aperture, setting a fundamental limit on resolving power.

quiz.q: What does the Rayleigh criterion define?
options: The total mass of an optical instrument
The maximum possible speed of light in any medium
The exact colour of light emitted by a star
The minimum angular separation at which two point sources can be resolved as separate

quiz.q: What physical phenomenon underlies the resolution limit described by the Rayleigh criterion?
options: The complete absence of any light entering the instrument
Gravitational lensing around a distant star
Radioactive decay within the instrument itself
Diffraction produced by the instruments aperture

quiz.q: What does resolving power describe for an optical instrument?
options: Its ability to change the colour of incoming light
Its total weight and physical size
Its capacity to store electrical energy
Its ability to distinguish closely spaced objects as separate

quiz.q: How does aperture size generally affect resolving power according to the Rayleigh criterion?
options: A larger aperture generally improves resolving power
A larger aperture always worsens resolving power
Aperture size has no effect on resolving power at all
Resolving power depends only on the colour of the instrument

quiz.q: Why does diffraction, rather than lens imperfection alone, set a fundamental limit on resolution?
options: Diffraction is an intrinsic wave effect present even in a perfect, flawless optical system
Diffraction can always be eliminated by using a larger lens
Diffraction only occurs in instruments with significant lens defects
Diffraction has no connection to the wave nature of light

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: The Serial Novel: Dickens and Publication in Instalments
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: the serial novel was published in regular instalments, often monthly, in newspapers or magazines, a format popularized by writers such as Charles Dickens that shaped narrative pacing through cliffhangers and episodic structure suited to a paying, ongoing readership.

quiz.q: How was a serial novel typically published?
options: Only after the authors death, with no instalments
In regular instalments, often monthly, in newspapers or magazines
As a single complete volume with no instalments at all
Exclusively as a private, unpublished manuscript

quiz.q: Which nineteenth-century writer is closely associated with popularizing the serial novel format?
options: Emily Dickinson
Homer
Charles Dickens
Sophocles

quiz.q: What narrative device did serial publication commonly encourage at the end of an instalment?
options: A complete resolution with no remaining tension
A detailed appendix of footnotes
A blank page with no content at all
A cliffhanger

quiz.q: How did serial publication shape a novels overall structure?
options: It eliminated the need for any structure whatsoever
It encouraged an episodic structure suited to the pacing of each instalment
It required the entire novel to be written and revealed at once
It forced every novel to have exactly one chapter

quiz.q: Why might serial publication have influenced an authors relationship with their readers?
options: Authors were legally forbidden from responding to reader reaction
An ongoing, paying readership could shape the reception and even the direction of the unfolding story
Readers had no access to a serialized novel until it was fully finished
Serial publication removed all contact between author and reader

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Discrete Math: Spanning Trees and Kruskals Algorithm
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: a spanning tree of a connected graph is a subgraph that includes every vertex and is itself a tree, and Kruskals algorithm constructs a minimum-weight spanning tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that does not create a cycle.

quiz.q: What is a spanning tree of a connected graph?
options: A subgraph that includes every vertex of the graph and is itself a tree
A graph that contains every possible cycle
A single isolated vertex with no edges at all
A subgraph that excludes most of the graphs vertices

quiz.q: What does Kruskals algorithm construct?
options: A minimum-weight spanning tree
The graph with the maximum possible number of cycles
A completely disconnected version of the original graph
A list of every vertex with no edges included

quiz.q: What rule does Kruskals algorithm follow when selecting edges to add?
options: It always removes the most expensive edge first
It adds every edge in the graph regardless of weight
It selects edges at random with no rule at all
It repeatedly adds the cheapest edge that does not create a cycle

quiz.q: Why must a valid spanning tree contain no cycles?
options: Acyclic graphs cannot be connected under any circumstances
Cycles are required for a graph to be considered a tree
Spanning trees are permitted to contain any number of cycles
A tree, by definition, is connected and acyclic

quiz.q: How does Kruskals algorithm build on the graph theory basics of vertices and edges studied earlier?
options: It replaces vertices and edges with an entirely different structure
It has no relationship to vertices or edges at all
It only applies to graphs with no edges whatsoever
It builds directly on that vertex and edge structure to select a minimal connecting subset of edges

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Vectors: Using the Cross Product to Find a Perpendicular Vector
subjects.summary: Compute the cross product of two 3D vectors to generate a vector perpendicular to both, and verify the result using the dot product.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Vectors: Using the Cross Product to Find a Perpendicular Vector

quiz.q: Find a × b for a = (1, 0, 0) and b = (0, 1, 0).
Find u × v for u = (2, 3, 4) and v = (5, 6, 7).
Given p = (1, −2, 3) and q = (2, 0, −1), compute p × q.
The vector n = a × b, where a = (3, 1, −2), is computed to be n = (10, −8, 11). Which calculation correctly verifies that n is perpendicular to a, and what should it equal?
options: a·n = 3(10) + 1(−8) + (−2)(11); the result should equal 1
|a| × |n| should equal |a × n|
a·n = 3(10) + 1(−8) + (−2)(11); the result should equal 0
a + n, computed component-wise, should equal the zero vector

quiz.q: Which vector is perpendicular to both c = (1, 1, 0) and d = (1, −1, 0)?

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: The Thomson Effect and Thermoelectric Circuits
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Thomson effect describes the heating or cooling that occurs when an electric current flows through a conductor along which a temperature gradient already exists, a third thermoelectric phenomenon alongside the Seebeck and Peltier effects studied earlier in this course.

quiz.q: What does the Thomson effect describe?
options: A phenomenon that occurs only in a perfect vacuum with no conductor
Heating or cooling that occurs when current flows through a conductor with an existing temperature gradient
The complete absence of heat transfer in any conductor
A change in a materials colour caused by an electric current

quiz.q: What must already exist along a conductor for the Thomson effect to occur?
options: An external magnetic field with no current involved
A complete absence of any electric current
A perfectly uniform temperature throughout
A temperature gradient

quiz.q: Alongside which two thermoelectric effects studied earlier does the Thomson effect belong?
options: The Hall effect and the Coriolis effect
The Seebeck effect and the Peltier effect
The photoelectric effect and the Zeeman effect
The Doppler effect and the Compton effect

quiz.q: What direction of energy transfer can the Thomson effect produce in a current-carrying conductor?
options: Only cooling, under every possible condition
Either heating or cooling, depending on the direction of current relative to the temperature gradient
No energy transfer of any kind, regardless of conditions
Only heating, under every possible condition

quiz.q: Why are the Seebeck, Peltier, and Thomson effects grouped together as thermoelectric phenomena?
options: They describe interactions between light and matter, not heat and current
They only apply to conductors at absolute zero temperature
They describe entirely unrelated phenomena with no shared theme
Each describes a distinct interaction between heat flow and electric current in a conductor

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: English Review: Detective Fiction, Naturalism, and Popular Forms
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand review: students revisit the mock-epic, the pastoral tradition, detective fiction and the golden age whodunit, literary naturalism, and memoir and the art of life writing.

quiz.q: What does a mock-epic typically do with the grand conventions of epic poetry?
options: Removes all poetic devices from the epic form
Turns the epic into a private diary with no audience
Uses them only to describe genuine historical battles
Applies them to a trivial or minor subject to create a comic, satirical effect

quiz.q: What does the pastoral tradition typically idealize?
options: The corruption of royal courts with no counterpoint
The complexity and noise of city life
Industrial machinery and urban commerce
Rural life and nature, often voiced through shepherd or rustic figures

quiz.q: What structure typically defines golden age detective fiction?
options: A story with no crime or mystery of any kind
A tale told entirely without a detective figure
A puzzle-like mystery solved through logical deduction from carefully planted clues
A narrative that reveals the culprit before any investigation begins

quiz.q: What forces do naturalist novels typically emphasize as shaping character?
options: Supernatural forces such as ghosts and spirits
Heredity, environment, and social forces beyond the characters control
Pure random chance with no underlying pattern at all
Only the characters own free choices, with no outside influence

quiz.q: What does memoir typically reconstruct?
options: A purely fictional life invented for entertainment
A biography of a person the author has never met
A specific period or theme from the authors own life
A complete, chronological record of an entire life from birth to the present

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: AdvancedFunctions Review: Statistics, Algebra, and Graph Theory
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand review: students revisit the Poisson distribution, the law of quadratic reciprocity, group theory, Boolean algebra and logic gates, and correlation and the Pearson correlation coefficient.

quiz.q: What kind of events does the Poisson distribution typically model?
options: Events that always occur at exactly the same time
Only events with a probability of exactly one half
Events with no possible variation whatsoever
Rare, independent events occurring a certain number of times in a fixed interval

quiz.q: What does the law of quadratic reciprocity relate?
options: The sum of two unrelated even numbers
Whether p is a quadratic residue modulo q to whether q is a quadratic residue modulo p
The value of an unrelated trigonometric identity
The number of divisors of a composite number only

quiz.q: What four properties define a group under its operation?
options: Commutativity alone, with no identity element required
A requirement that the set contain exactly one element
Only closure, with no other requirements
Closure, associativity, an identity element, and inverses for every element

quiz.q: What values does Boolean algebra fundamentally operate on?
options: Negative fractions only
True and false (or one and zero) values
Only irrational numbers
Complex numbers exclusively

quiz.q: What does the Pearson correlation coefficient measure?
options: The strength and direction of the linear relationship between two quantitative variables
The total number of data points collected
The exact mean of a single data set
The mode of a categorical variable

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Number Theory: The Euclidean Algorithm and Greatest Common Divisor
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Math strand: the Euclidean algorithm finds the greatest common divisor of two integers by repeatedly dividing and taking remainders until a remainder of zero is reached, offering a faster method than listing every factor.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Number Theory: The Euclidean Algorithm and Greatest Common Divisor

quiz.q: What does the Euclidean algorithm calculate?
options: The sum of two unrelated fractions
The exact prime factorization of a single number
The greatest common divisor of two integers
The least common multiple of every integer

quiz.q: How does the Euclidean algorithm proceed?
options: By guessing an answer with no calculation involved
By multiplying the two numbers together repeatedly
By repeatedly dividing and taking remainders until a remainder of zero is reached
By listing every possible factor of both numbers first

quiz.q: What is the greatest common divisor of two numbers when the Euclidean algorithm stops?
options: Always the larger of the two original numbers
The sum of both original numbers
Always the number one, regardless of the inputs
The last nonzero remainder produced during the process

quiz.q: Why might the Euclidean algorithm be preferred over listing all factors of large numbers?
options: It always produces an incorrect answer for large numbers
Listing factors is always faster for every possible number
It finds the greatest common divisor more quickly, especially for large integers
The Euclidean algorithm cannot be used on large numbers at all

quiz.q: What is the greatest common divisor of 24 and 36, found using the Euclidean algorithm?

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Physics Review: Fluid, Optical, and Electromagnetic Effects
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand review: students revisit the Magnus effect, the Venturi effect and Bernoullis principle, total internal reflection, Newtons rings, and the Tyndall effect.

quiz.q: What is the Magnus effect?
options: The complete absence of drag on a spinning object
The tendency of an object to fall in a perfectly straight line
The curved path taken by a spinning object moving through a fluid, caused by a sideways lift force
A magnetic force acting on any moving object

quiz.q: What does the Venturi effect describe?
options: A drop in fluid pressure as the fluid speeds up through a constricted section of a pipe
The complete stopping of fluid flow at a constriction
A rise in fluid pressure whenever a pipe widens
A change in fluid temperature with no change in pressure

quiz.q: What is total internal reflection?
options: A phenomenon that only occurs with sound waves
Light reflecting entirely back into a denser medium when it strikes a boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle
The complete absorption of light at any surface
Light passing completely unaffected through any boundary

quiz.q: What pattern do Newtons rings form?
options: Concentric bright and dark circular fringes
A uniform, unchanging field of one colour
A random, non-repeating scatter of colour
A single straight bright line with no pattern

quiz.q: What is the Tyndall effect?
options: The scattering of light by particles suspended in a colloid, making a beam of light visible from the side
The complete absorption of all light by a transparent solution
The bending of light as it passes through a single flat pane of glass
A phenomenon that only occurs in a perfect vacuum

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: The Sestina: A Fixed Form Built on Repeated End-Words
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: a sestina is a fixed poetic form of six six-line stanzas plus a three-line envoi, in which the same six end-words recur in a fixed rotating pattern across every stanza instead of relying on rhyme, generating meaning through the shifting context of repetition.

quiz.q: What structural feature defines a sestina rather than a rhyme scheme?
options: Every line must rhyme with the line before it
The same six end-words recur in a fixed rotating pattern across every stanza
The poem must contain exactly fourteen lines
Every stanza must use a completely different set of words

quiz.q: How many six-line stanzas does a standard sestina contain before its closing section?
options: Six
Four
Three
Ten

quiz.q: What is the short closing stanza of a sestina called?
options: The envoi
The coda
The refrain
The volta

quiz.q: How does meaning shift across a sestina even though the same end-words repeat?
options: The words meanings are fixed and never change in any way
The changing context and position of each repeated word generates new shades of meaning
Repetition in a sestina always removes all meaning from the poem
Each stanza replaces the end-words with a synonym

quiz.q: Why might the sestinas rigid word-repetition pattern appeal to a poet writing about obsession or memory?
options: Sestinas are only ever used for comic subjects
Rigid forms cannot be used to explore psychological subject matter
The compulsive return of the same words can mirror a mind circling the same ideas
The form requires the poet to avoid repeating any idea

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Statistics: Confidence Intervals and Estimating a Population Parameter
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: a confidence interval uses sample data to construct a range of plausible values for an unknown population parameter, paired with a confidence level that describes how often intervals built this way would capture the true parameter across repeated sampling.

quiz.q: What does a confidence interval provide an estimate of?
options: The size of the sample used in a study
The exact, guaranteed value of a population parameter
A range of plausible values for an unknown population parameter
A single data point drawn at random

quiz.q: What does a 95 percent confidence level describe?
options: That 95 percent of the population was directly measured
That about 95 percent of intervals built this way, across repeated sampling, would capture the true parameter
That there is a 95 percent chance the parameter equals the sample mean exactly
That the interval is wrong 95 percent of the time

quiz.q: What generally happens to a confidence intervals width as the sample size increases?
options: The interval always widens without exception
The interval size is unrelated to sample size
The interval collapses to a single value at any sample size
The interval tends to narrow, reflecting more precise estimation

quiz.q: Which earlier-studied concept is typically used to help construct a confidence interval around a sample mean?
options: The range between the smallest and largest data values only
A single outlier value from the sample
The standard error, drawing on properties of the sampling distribution
The mode of the raw data set alone

quiz.q: Why is a confidence interval generally more informative than reporting a single point estimate alone?
options: It conveys the uncertainty around the estimate, not just one plausible value
A point estimate always contains more information than any interval
Point estimates are always more precise than interval estimates
Confidence intervals remove the need for any sample data

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Geometry: Vector Projections and Scalar Components
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Math strand: the projection of one vector onto another describes how much of the first vector points in the direction of the second, and it can be calculated using the dot product together with the magnitude of the vector being projected onto.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Geometry: Vector Projections and Scalar Components

quiz.q: What does the projection of one vector onto another describe?
options: The total length of both vectors added together
How much of the first vector points in the direction of the second
The colour associated with each vector
The number of dimensions a vector exists in

quiz.q: What mathematical tool is used to calculate a vector projection?
options: The dot product, together with the magnitude of the vector being projected onto
A random number generator
Only the sum of the two vectors
Only the difference of the two vectors magnitudes

quiz.q: If two vectors are perpendicular, what is the projection of one onto the other?
options: Always a negative number
Zero, since perpendicular vectors have no component in each others direction
Undefined and impossible to calculate
Equal to the length of the longer vector

quiz.q: The scalar component of a projection represents what kind of quantity?
options: A count of how many vectors exist in a diagram
A magnitude with a sign, indicating size and direction along the target vector
A fixed constant that never changes between problems
A colour value with no numerical meaning

quiz.q: Vector projections are useful in physics for calculating what kind of quantity?
options: The temperature of an object in motion
The component of a force acting in a specific direction
The name of the object being measured
The exact colour of a moving object

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Chaos Theory and Sensitive Dependence on Initial Conditions
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: chaos theory studies deterministic systems whose long-term behaviour is extremely sensitive to tiny differences in initial conditions, so that two nearly identical starting states can diverge into wildly different outcomes, popularly illustrated by the butterfly effect.

quiz.q: What defining property do chaotic systems display with respect to their starting conditions?
options: Extreme sensitivity, so tiny differences in initial conditions lead to wildly different outcomes
A guarantee that outcomes never change over time
Identical long-term behaviour regardless of starting point
Complete independence from their initial conditions

quiz.q: What popular name is often used for sensitive dependence on initial conditions?
options: The butterfly effect
The photoelectric effect
The domino effect
The observer effect

quiz.q: Are chaotic systems considered random, given their unpredictable long-term behaviour?
options: No, they are deterministic; unpredictability arises from sensitivity, not randomness
Yes, chaotic systems are governed entirely by random chance
Chaos theory only applies to systems with no rules whatsoever
Chaotic systems have no governing equations at all

quiz.q: Why does sensitive dependence make long-term prediction difficult for a chaotic system, even though its equations are known exactly?
options: Long-term prediction is always easy for chaotic systems
Chaotic systems have no measurable initial state at all
The equations governing the system are always unknown
Any tiny measurement error in the initial state grows rapidly, making distant forecasts unreliable

quiz.q: Which real-world system is commonly cited as an example where chaos theory limits long-range predictability?
options: A single stationary object at rest
A perfectly isolated, unchanging vacuum
Weather and atmospheric systems
An object with no interacting forces of any kind

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: The Historical Novel: Reimagining the Past in Fiction
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: the historical novel sets its story in a real past period, blending researched historical detail with invented characters and plot, using the gap between documented fact and imaginative reconstruction to explore how the past can be understood and represented.

quiz.q: What defines a historical novel as a genre?
options: A story that only ever occurs in an imagined future
A story set in a real past period, blending researched detail with invented characters and plot
A form that requires every event to be entirely factual
A text that refuses to include any invented characters

quiz.q: What gap does the historical novel often explore imaginatively?
options: The gap between prose and dramatic dialogue only
The gap between two entirely fictional worlds
The gap between two unrelated poetic forms
The gap between documented historical fact and imaginative reconstruction

quiz.q: What kind of research typically supports a historical novels setting and detail?
options: Research into the real historical period being depicted
No research is typically required for this genre
Research into a future period that has not yet occurred
Research exclusively into unrelated scientific theories

quiz.q: How does the historical novel differ from historiographic metafiction, studied in an earlier batch?
options: The historical novel generally reconstructs the past more straightforwardly, while historiographic metafiction foregrounds and questions the act of historical narration itself
The historical novel never includes any real historical events
Historiographic metafiction cannot be set in the past at all
The two genres are entirely identical in every respect

quiz.q: Why might a novelist choose invented characters to narrate real historical events?
options: Invented characters remove any possibility of historical detail
Invented characters can move through history with a flexibility and interiority real documented figures may not allow
Historical fiction is legally required to avoid all real events
Invented characters are never permitted to interact with real historical events

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Solving Exponential Equations Using Logarithms
subjects.summary: Students solve exponential equations that cannot be rewritten with a common base by applying logarithms to both sides, using the power law of logarithms to isolate the variable.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Solving Exponential Equations Using Logarithms

quiz.q: To solve 5^x = 40 for x, an appropriate first step is:
options: Take the logarithm of both sides
Divide both sides by 5
Square both sides
Add 5 to both sides

quiz.q: Solve 3^x = 20 for x, rounded to two decimal places.
Solve 2^(x+1) = 15 for x.
When solving an exponential equation using logs, which log law allows moving the exponent to the front?
options: Power law
Change of base law
Product law
Quotient law

quiz.q: Solve 7^(2x) = 50 for x, rounded to three decimal places.

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Data Management: Bayes Theorem and Updating Probabilities
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Math strand: Bayes Theorem provides a method for updating the probability of an event as new evidence becomes available, building directly on the idea of conditional probability introduced earlier in the course.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Data Management: Bayes Theorem and Updating Probabilities

quiz.q: What does Bayes Theorem allow you to do?
options: Eliminate the need for probability altogether
Calculate the area of any triangle
Update the probability of an event based on new evidence
Determine the exact value of an unrelated variable

quiz.q: Bayes Theorem builds most directly on which earlier probability concept?
options: The dot product of vectors
The Pythagorean Theorem
Conditional probability
Synthetic division

quiz.q: In Bayes Theorem, what happens to an initial probability estimate once new evidence is considered?
options: It is revised to produce an updated, more informed probability
It is always discarded and replaced with zero
It remains completely unchanged regardless of new evidence
It is converted into an unrelated geometric shape

quiz.q: Why is Bayes Theorem useful in fields such as medical testing?
options: It helps estimate the true likelihood of a condition after accounting for a test result
It eliminates the need for any medical testing altogether
It has no application to medicine or testing of any kind
It guarantees a test result is always accurate with no uncertainty

quiz.q: What is required before Bayes Theorem can be applied to a problem?
options: A list of unrelated historical dates
A guarantee that the event in question is impossible
Some known or estimated probabilities relating the event and the evidence
A completed geometric proof with no probability involved

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: Muon Decay and Experimental Proof of Time Dilation
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: muons produced by cosmic rays high in the atmosphere have such a short lifetime that classical physics predicts almost none should reach the ground, yet many are detected at sea level, a discrepancy explained by relativistic time dilation extending their apparent lifetime as observed from the ground.

quiz.q: What is surprising, from a purely classical standpoint, about muons reaching the ground?
options: Muons are classically predicted to never form in the atmosphere
Muons are classically predicted to survive indefinitely with no decay at all
Classical physics predicts muons cannot be detected under any conditions
Their extremely short lifetime should let almost none survive the trip from the upper atmosphere to sea level

quiz.q: What relativistic effect explains why far more muons reach the ground than classical physics predicts?
options: Time dilation, which extends the muons apparent lifetime as observed from the ground
The photoelectric effect converting muons into photons
Gravitational lensing bending the muons path
A complete absence of any effect; the classical prediction was correct all along

quiz.q: Where are the muons studied in this classic experiment typically produced?
options: On the surface of the sun
Inside a laboratory vacuum chamber at rest
Deep underground in a nuclear reactor
High in the atmosphere, through collisions caused by cosmic rays

quiz.q: Why is the muon decay experiment considered strong evidence for special relativity?
options: It has no connection to relativity and is explained entirely by classical mechanics
It disproves time dilation rather than supporting it
It provides a directly observable, quantitative confirmation of time dilation using naturally occurring particles
It only applies to particles at rest with no motion involved

quiz.q: From the reference frame of the muon itself, how is the same survival result explained?
options: The muon simply does not decay in its own reference frame
The muon experiences no time at all under any circumstances
The ground moves away from the muon at the speed of light
Length contraction shortens the distance to the ground that the muon must travel

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Drama: Verbatim Theatre and the Rhetoric of Real Speech
subjects.summary: Explores documentary and verbatim theatre, where scripts are built word-for-word from interviews, testimony, or public records, and considers the ethical and rhetorical choices playwrights make when staging real people's words.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Drama: Verbatim Theatre and the Rhetoric of Real Speech

quiz.q: Verbatim theatre is distinguished from other drama primarily because its dialogue:
options: Must be performed without any script at all
Is composed entirely of invented characters' speech
Is drawn directly from real interviews, testimony, or public records
Is written only in strict verse form

quiz.q: A key ethical question verbatim playwrights face when editing real testimony is:
options: Whether to use present or past tense throughout
How much can be cut or rearranged before the speaker's original meaning is distorted
Which font to use for the stage directions
Whether the play needs an intermission

quiz.q: Verbatim theatre most closely overlaps with which nonfiction tradition studied elsewhere in this course?
options: The personal eulogy
New Journalism and literary reportage
The annotated bibliography
The extended metaphor essay

quiz.q: Why might a director cast actors to embody real speakers rather than simply play recordings in a verbatim production?
options: Actors are required to improvise well beyond the transcript
Live embodiment creates dramatic presence while still anchoring dialogue in documented words
Recordings are legally prohibited in all theatre
It removes the need for a script entirely

quiz.q: Which of the following is a risk verbatim theatre runs that wholly invented drama does not?
options: Overusing metaphor in dialogue
Misrepresenting a real, identifiable person through selective editing
Losing the audience's attention during a long scene
Failing to follow a three-act structure

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Exponential Growth and Decay: Modelling Real-World Situations
subjects.summary: Students construct and interpret exponential growth and decay models for contexts such as population growth, radioactive decay, and depreciation, and solve for time, rate, or initial amount within the model.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Exponential Growth and Decay: Modelling Real-World Situations

quiz.q: A population of 2000 grows at 3% per year. Which model represents the population after t years?
A radioactive sample decays according to A(t) = A0(0.5)^(t/h), where h is the half-life. If A0 = 100 g and h = 10 days, how much remains after 30 days?
A car worth $25,000 depreciates 15% per year. Which expression gives its value after 4 years?
For continuous growth modelled by A(t) = A0 e^(kt) with k = 0.05, what does k represent?
options: The half-life
The doubling time
The continuous growth rate per unit time
The initial amount

quiz.q: A bacteria culture doubles every 3 hours starting at 500. How many bacteria are present after 9 hours?

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Calculus: Implicit Differentiation
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: implicit differentiation is a technique for finding the derivative of a relation in which y is not isolated as a function of x, by differentiating both sides of an equation with respect to x and applying the chain rule to terms involving y.

quiz.q: When is implicit differentiation typically used?
options: Only when working with whole numbers
Only when an equation has no variables at all
When y is not isolated as a function of x in an equation
Only when a function is already fully simplified for y

quiz.q: What technique is applied to terms involving y during implicit differentiation?
options: Basic long division
The Pythagorean Theorem
The chain rule
The quadratic formula

quiz.q: What is the general first step in implicit differentiation?

subjects.summary: Grade 8 Science strand: quantum physics studies the behaviour of extremely small particles, such as electrons, which can behave differently than larger objects described by everyday physics.

subjects.subject: English

A performance requiring an entirely new set of characters every single time
Largely improvised performance built around recurring stock characters

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Discrete Math: Recurrence Relations and Solving Linear Recurrences
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: a recurrence relation defines each term of a sequence in terms of earlier terms, and a linear recurrence with constant coefficients can be solved explicitly by finding the roots of an associated characteristic polynomial, generalizing the Fibonacci-style sequences studied earlier.

A single fixed constant with no sequence involved

Fibonacci-style sequences defined by earlier terms
A sequence containing only the number zero
A sequence with no defined pattern whatsoever

quiz.q: What information, besides the recurrence relation itself, is needed to fully determine a sequence?
options: The final term of an infinite sequence
No additional information is ever required
The average of all terms in the sequence

quiz.q: Why are linear recurrences with constant coefficients useful in modelling real growth processes?
options: They can only model quantities that never change over time
They have no application outside of pure abstract mathematics

subjects.subject: Calculus

subjects.subject: Physics
subjects.title: The Fizeau Experiment and the Speed of Light in Moving Water
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Physics strand: the Fizeau experiment measured how the speed of light changes when light travels through water that is itself flowing, finding a partial rather than full addition of the waters velocity to the lights speed, an early result later explained by special relativitys velocity addition formula.

quiz.q: What did the Fizeau experiment measure?
options: The magnetic properties of still water
The exact mass of a water molecule
The boiling point of water at high altitude
How the speed of light changes when travelling through flowing water

quiz.q: Which later theory fully explained the partial velocity addition observed by Fizeau?

The theory of gravitation developed by Newton
Special relativitys velocity addition formula

quiz.q: Why is the Fizeau experiment considered historically important for the development of relativity?
options: It confirmed that light behaves identically to a simple classical particle in every situation
It disproved the existence of light entirely

It provided no evidence relevant to the study of light or motion

quiz.q: What medium did light travel through in the original Fizeau experiment?

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: The Literature Review: Synthesizing a Field of Research
subjects.summary: Grade 12 English strand: a literature review surveys and synthesizes existing scholarship on a topic, organizing sources thematically or chronologically to identify trends, agreements, and gaps, distinct from a research essay because its primary goal is mapping a field rather than arguing a single original thesis.

quiz.q: What is the primary goal of a literature review?
options: To survey and synthesize existing scholarship on a topic
To retell a novels plot from beginning to end
To argue a single narrow thesis with no reference to other sources

quiz.q: How are sources commonly organized within a literature review?
options: Alphabetically by the readers own name
By the physical length of each source only
Thematically or chronologically

quiz.q: What might a well-constructed literature review help a researcher identify?

The exact opposite of what every source actually argues
A topic with no existing scholarship of any kind

quiz.q: How does a literature review differ from a standard research essay, as studied in an earlier batch?

It is required to contain the projects final conclusion
It establishes what is already known and where the writers own contribution might fit

subjects.subject: AdvancedFunctions
subjects.title: Number Theory: Continued Fractions and Best Rational Approximations
subjects.summary: Grade 12 Advanced Functions strand: a continued fraction expresses a real number as a nested sequence of integer and reciprocal terms, and truncating this expansion produces the best possible rational approximations to that number for a given denominator size, a property exploited in both pure number theory and practical approximation.

quiz.q: What does a continued fraction express a real number as?

options: They only ever equal the original number exactly, with no approximation involved

options: An expansion with no integer terms at all

subjects.subject: Calculus

subjects.subject: Physics

A strong fit within the data guarantees perfect predictions at any distance from that data

subjects.subject: Calculus
subjects.title: Calculus Preview: Continuity of Functions
subjects.summary: Grade 9 Math strand: a function is continuous at a point if its graph has no break, jump, or hole there, meaning the limit of the function as it approaches that point equals the actual value of the function at that point.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a function to be continuous at a point?
options: The graph must always be a straight line
The function only exists for negative numbers
The function is undefined at every single point
Its graph has no break, jump, or hole at that point

quiz.q: For a function to be continuous at a point, its limit at that point must equal what?
options: Zero, regardless of the function
The largest value the function ever reaches
A value chosen at random with no connection to the function
The actual value of the function at that point

quiz.q: Which of these would indicate a function is not continuous at a specific point?
options: A hole or gap in the graph at that point
A smooth curve with no interruptions
A function defined everywhere with matching limits
A straight line with no breaks

Limits can only be calculated for continuous functions, never any other kind
Continuity and limits are entirely unrelated mathematical ideas

quiz.q: A function that is continuous over an entire interval can generally be drawn how?
options: Without lifting a pen from the paper across that interval
Only by using a ruler with no curves allowed
Only if the function is a straight line
